articles.title: I recently tested the flagship Dreame X50 Ultra Complete robot vacuum and was impressed by its cleaning capabilities — and it's $200 off in this early Black Friday deal
articles.content: As a Reviews Writer here at Tom's Guide, I spend most of my time testing out the latest robot vacuums . Now, they say never to work with children or animals, but that's where the Dreame X50 Ultra Complete thrives — it makes sure all the mess they leave in their wake is taken care of. Since recommending this robot vacuum to a friend with children and pets in her home, it's great to see a $200 price drop on the flagship robot vacuum in this early Black Friday deal . You can now purchase the Dreame X50 Ultra Complete for $1,099 on Amazon . It's an impressive gadget that's pretty much self-sufficient and can even climb over small inclines with retractable legs. It excels on hard floors and can mop up any mess with its circular mop pads. The Dreame X50 Ultra Complete excels on hard floors with its side-sweeping arms, mapping navigation, low-maintenance base station, user-friendly app, and stylish design. View Deal My favorite thing about this robot vacuum is the extended reach. Most standard vacuums try their best to get ot the edges of the room, but almost always miss the corners. The Dreame X50 Ultra Complete is a little different because its side-sweeping arms and mop pads can get into all the gaps the robot can't quite get to. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Speaking of getting into small spaces, the sensor on top of the vacuum is retractable. This means that it can easily get under low furniture up to 3.54 inches high. During testing, it easily made its way under my low-lying sofa, and the LED lighting came on to guide the way. (Image credit: Tom's Guide / Millie Fender) The retractable legs are the real star of the show here. They help the robot make its way over small ledges, high-pile carpets, and even obstacles like table legs. It's a very helpful assistant to have in the house and makes cleanup after a busy day much easier. You can find out more about the robot vacuum by reading my full Dreame X50 Ultra Complete review .

articles.title: Stop doing sit-ups — a yoga instructor and strength and conditioning coach recommends this exercise to work the core, hip flexors, and back muscles
articles.content: Did you know that when it comes to building core strength and stability, sit-ups and crunches aren’t the best place to start? Unless you perform them with perfect form, sit-ups and crunches can stress your lower back and neck because you repeatedly bend your spine forward under load. What’s more, if, like me, you’re a runner or spend a lot of time sitting behind a desk, there’s a high chance your hip flexors take over during this move. This can pull on your lower back, causing discomfort. Instead, yoga instructor and strength and conditioning coach Melissa Leach recommends a simple yoga pose to build deep core strength and spinal stability. Read on to find out more. As a reminder, if you’re a complete beginner, pregnant or postpartum, or returning to fitness following an injury or surgery, this might not be the right move for you and your body. It’s always best to seek personalized advice from a qualified professional. How to do boat pose The move Leach recommends over sit-ups and crunches is the boat pose. "Boat pose is one of the most efficient core exercises because it doesn't just isolate the abs; it engages the hip flexors, glutes, pelvic muscles, and back all at once, helping build functional core strength rather than working one single muscle in isolation,” she says. All you’ll need is your bodyweight, but using one of the best yoga mats can help make things more comfortable. “There are different ways to perform boat pose. Traditional holds usually consist of staying in the pose for a total of 25 breaths, broken into five sets, while others add movement by hinging the upper body upward and downward,” says Leach. “This version is a more accessible entry point for beginners, starting with bent knees and shorter, more manageable holds.” (Image credit: Future) Sit on the floor with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor Lean your torso back slightly while keeping your spine long and your chest lifted Engage your core and slowly lift your feet off the floor, bringing your shins parallel to the ground Balance on your sit bones, avoiding rolling onto your tailbone Once stable, extend your arms in front of you, with your palms facing each other at shoulder height If you feel comfortable, you can slowly extend your legs to create a ‘V’ shape with your body Hold for 20-30 seconds, and repeat 2-4 times “For beginners, keeping your legs bent in a half boat pose instead of straight can help reduce the core strain and effort required at the start. Lightly gripping the backs of your thighs can also provide support to help you balance,” says Leach. “If you struggle with balance and maintaining a straight spine, you can either sit on a folded blanket or cushion to help tilt the pelvis forward, or sit with your back a few inches from the wall for reassurance. “The most important thing is to get a hold of the technique first, so start slowly, only holding for as long as it's comfortable and slowly increasing the length as your core strength improves.” What are the benefits? On paper, this move looks simple, but after 20 seconds, you’ll know it’s anything but. Holding your torso and legs lifted activates your rectus abdominis (six-pack muscles), obliques, and deeper transverse abdominis at the same time. You’ll also work the muscles along your spine, counteracting bad posture from prolonged sitting. (Image credit: Shutterstock) As you hold your legs off the floor, you’ll work your hip flexors, quadriceps, and inner thighs, as well as working your balance and coordination. "Boat pose also helps build stability rather than just endurance. Holding the position forces your deep core muscles, the ones that support your spine and pelvis, to switch on and stay engaged throughout. Over time, this can translate into better posture, a stronger lower back, and a core that supports your everyday movement," Leach adds. articles.title: Hate dragging out the ladder? Clear your gutters from the ground with these 3 vacuum attachments instead
articles.content: Few home maintenance chores feel more daunting than clearing clogged gutters. Dragging an extension ladder across uneven flowerbeds, leaning precariously over shrubs, and scooping wet sludge by hand is both exhausting and genuinely dangerous. Ignoring the buildup is not an option either, as overflowing gutters quickly send rainwater pouring down your siding and pooling against your foundation. The trick to clearing your roofline safely comes down to extending your reach from the ground, removing loose debris before you add water, and knowing when a clog is too stubborn for a pole attachment. Why you shouldn't put off cleaning clogged gutters As damp leaves and pine needles pack together, they form a heavy dam that blocks rainwater from reaching the downspouts. That trapped water spills over the lip of the trough, soaking fascia boards until the wood rots and saturating the soil around your foundation walls, where leaks and basement dampness soon follow. In colder months, standing water inside a blocked gutter also freezes solid, adding enough weight to pull brackets loose from the roofline or form damaging ice dams under your shingles. Here are three simple ways to clear your gutters cleanly while keeping both feet firmly on the ground. The easy way to clear gutters from the ground 1. Pull dry debris out with a wet/dry vac gutter kit Blasting leaves out with a leaf blower works over open grass, yet it creates a mess over decks, patio furniture, or flowerbeds. A gutter attachment kit for a standard wet/dry shop vac keeps that debris contained while letting you work safely from the lawn. (Image credit: Craftsman ) Brands like Craftsman sell these universal kits at hardware stores and Amazon. Each kit includes three or four rigid plastic extension wands that click together into a 10-to-14-foot pole, topped with a curved, U-shaped nozzle. Hold the assembled pole like a pool skimmer, hook the curved nozzle over the gutter lip, and switch the vacuum on to pull dry leaves, twigs, and grit straight down into the canister beside you. Work in short sections along the wall, lifting the hook over each gutter bracket as you walk , and wear eye protection and gloves in case stray debris drops from above. Gutter Cleaning Attachment Kit: $27 This four-piece accessory kit fits Craftsman and most other wet/dry vacs with a 2-1/2-inch hose, giving you two rigid extension wands, a curved gutter nozzle for suction, and a blower nozzle to clear dry leaves safely from the ground. View Deal 2. Lift stubborn clumps with a telescopic gutter scoop If your debris is too damp for a vacuum to lift, grabbing a hose right away will only turn the leaves into heavy, wet paste. (Image credit: Shutterstock) Instead, attach a curved gutter scoop or stiff brush to a telescopic extension pole suited to your roofline height. Work in short sections and focus on lifting material up and out of the channel rather than pushing it toward the downspout , which only packs debris tighter into the outlet. If you cannot see over the lip of the trough, clipping a small pole-mounted inspection camera to the shaft lets you spot any leftover buildup without guessing. 3. Flush the channel gently with a curved hose wand Once you have removed the bulk of the leaves, you still need to clear fine shingle grit and confirm that water can actually escape down the pipe. (Image credit: Shutterstock) Hook a curved garden-hose attachment over the gutter lip and run a gentle stream of water rather than a high-pressure blast , which can loosen gutter brackets or force water up under your shingles. Work toward the downspout to wash remaining dirt away. If water starts backing up over the edge, turn the hose off immediately rather than adding more water, as a persistent blockage inside the downspout elbow usually needs to be cleared by hand. articles.title: 3 acclaimed sci-fi movies on HBO Max with 90% or higher on Rotten Tomatoes — including a Stanley Kubrick classic that changed the medium
articles.content: As First World problems go, losing your evening to non-committal HBO Max scrolling isn't ideal. It's way too easy to just stick on your 14th "The Sopranos" rewatch on the HBO streaming service, rather than give a potential sci-fi classic you've never seen before a much-deserved (and overdue) viewing. That's where my obsessive cinephile colleagues and I are here for. We all watch movies with great passion. For me, it's what gets me out of bed in the morning. Though I don't always personally agree with Rotten Tomatoes ratings — how is "The Matrix" only at 83%?! — the trio of HBO Max pictures I've picked out for you are all excellent, and all scored at least 90% or higher. Anyway, the following three sci-fi flicks are all streaming now on HBO Max, and each one is stellar. So get them watched ASAP. ‘2001: A Space Odyssey’ (1968) It's utterly appalling that I only saw “2001: A Space Odyssey” for the first time post-COVID. Stanley Kubrick’s seminal sci-fi opus is a mind-bending watch in the best possible way. It looks incredible, the final act is both spellbinding and slightly mystifying, and it easily boasts one of the most iconic scores of all time. It’s a five-star masterpiece. Yet I shamefully knew of it first for cheeky references in 1994’s “Deep Space Homer” episode from our beloved Springfieldian family, then again during 2023’s “Barbie”, which features a lovely, genuinely funny callback to the iconic monolith scene. And I’d never seen the film at that point! Shameful! Just know that this is the defining Kubrick masterpiece. HAL! Those apes getting comfy up against the monolith! The all-time iconic final scene with the space baby! I know I said it before, but “seminal” really is the only word to describe “2001: A Space Odyssey”. It’s arguably the most important and influential sci-fi movie ever made. RT is doing Kubrick's opus dirty at ‘just’ a 91% rating. Rotten Tomatoes score: 91% Watch “2001: A Space Odyssey ” on HBO Max now 'Dune: Part Two' (2024) I’m fond of “Dune: Part Two”, just as I was of its 2021 predecessor — two movies that pretty much erased David Lynch’s polarizing 1984 version from memory banks. And Lynch rarely dealt in duds. Though I don’t consider him at the level of legendary cinematographer Roger Deakins (an occasional Denis Villeneuve collaborator), Greig Fraser still shoots the mid-part of this epic sci-fi trilogy gorgeously. Do I think “Dune: Part Two” is as good a picture as either Villeneuve’s 2016 “Arrival" (91% RT rating) or my beloved "Blade Runner 2049" (88% RT)? Hell no. But it’s a classy sci-fi sequel that has me all in on this December’s Dunesday. I can’t lie, though. I do think "Part Two" misses the wonderful presence of Duncan Idaho (Jason Momoa). But hey, we still get those colossal sandworms. And new Big Bad Feyd-Rautha Harkonnen (played with a delicious serpent-like venom by Austin Butler) proves a great foil for Paul Atredides. As for our moody duke, Timothée Chalamet continues to nail down his leading man status in films with real smarts. Rotten Tomatoes score: 92% Watch "Dune: Part Two" on HBO Max now ‘Dawn of the Planet of the Apes’ (2014) Can you quickly indulge me in a quick Rotten Tomatoes rant? The fact that “Dawn of the Planet of the Apes” is sitting on the same 91% rating as my favourite ever movie “Jurassic Park”... well, that’s frankly unhinged. The sequel to 2011’s successful franchise reboot “Rise of the Planet of the Apes”, “Dawn” is another well-meaning sci-fi with a heart, strong performances and excellent effects. It just ain’t Spielberg’s dino masterpiece. Rant over. With our simian hero Caesar (another impeccable mo-cap performance from Andy Serkis) now very much in charge of his clan of developed apes, the film’s central conflict occurs when a team of humans tries to repair a hydroelectric dam in monkey territory. Although initial exchanges go badly, the kindly-natured super chimp eventually lets Malcolm (a very good Jason Clarke) fix the dam, and a cross-species…

articles.title: Waking up at night is the biggest barrier to a good night's sleep for over 1,700 Tom's Guide readers — an insomnia expert explains how to stop it
articles.content: We all know how incredible it feels to wake up after a great night's sleep: refreshed, clear-headed and ready to tackle the day ahead. But for many people, nighttime wake-ups are impacting their ability to achieve that. In fact, in a Tom's Guide sleep poll, more than 1,700 of our readers said that waking up during the night it is their biggest barrier to getting good night's rest. The poll showed that this problem far outweighed any of the other common challenges to good sleep, including snoring , not being able to fall asleep sleep and overheating at night. So, to help address this widespread issue, we've spoken to Dr. Saema Tahir , a sleep and pulmonary specialist, to find out more about the affects of nighttime wake-ups, what steps you can take to curb them and how to fall back to sleep if you do find yourself wide awake in the middle of the night. What did the Tom’s Guide survey uncover about the impact of nighttime wake-ups on sleep? (Image credit: Future) Here at Tom's Guide we're running an ongoing sleep poll to find out what is stopping our readers from sleeping well. (Scroll below for your chance to have your say). For almost three months, the poll has asked 'What is your biggest barrier to getting a good night's sleep?' The results so far paint a clear picture of the major issue readers are facing when it comes to sleep: nighttime wake-ups. The overwhelming majority of respondents, currently 69% (more than 1,700 people) of those who have taken part in the poll, selected 'waking up during the night' as their response. ' Can't fall asleep ' comes in second at 17% of respondents, while 'overheating at night' affects 6% of respondents and 'snoring (you or your partner' and 'can't get comfortable' have each currently received 4% of votes in the poll. "There are a variety of different reasons that people wake up throughout the night. So I'm actually not surprised by the data," says Dr. Tahir, a quadruple board-certified sleep specialist, adding that it is "the number one complaint I see in the office as well." The sleep expert explains that that the reasons for nighttime wake-ups range "from behavioural, environmental, medical symptoms of undiagnosed disorders, and there's sleep disorders in themselves that can wake you up in the middle of the night." When is waking up at night a problem? (Image credit: Future) Clearly the results of our poll show that nighttime awakenings are impacting sleep quality for many people — so when exactly does waking at night become problem? A brief wake-up during the night isn't actually abnormal, research shows that it's actually part of how our sleep cycles work. During the course of the night, people typically go through as many as five sleep cycles — consisting of light sleep, deep sleep and REM sleep that typically last around 90-100 minutes each — and in between each cycle you may briefly awaken. What becomes problematic is something is waking you up or you are unable to go back to sleep. Dr. Saema Tahir "Wake ups, 3 to 4 times, sometimes 5 times a night, are normal. Most people do wake up. They just don't remember them. Or they're able to go right back to sleep. So that is a normal sleep process," says Dr. Tahir, who treats sleep issues including insomnia, circadian rhythm disorders and sleep apnea from her practice in New York. "What becomes problematic is something is waking you up or you are unable to go back to sleep. That's when we think of it as a potential problem, but most people don't realise that we all wake up." How does waking up at night impact your sleep? If you're waking up and not getting back to sleep, Dr. Tahir points out that firstly, you will not be clocking up enough sleep. "And if you're not getting enough hours, you're probably not getting the appropriate architecture. So, you are missing out on, probably, the deeper stages of sleep," she explains. articles.title: I tried this 7-minute micro-workout before every shower for 30 days — is it worth the hype?
articles.content: If you haven't heard of "micromovement" routines, it's like exercise snacking , where you break up sedentary time with mini workouts or chunks of movement, like walks, bodyweight routines, or even a quick jog. According to research from Yoga-Go , you may add eight years to your biological age if you spend a lot of time sitting, which can be eight hours a day or more, regardless of whether you still exercise daily. Determined to start my day on the right foot, I decided to add a seven-minute bodyweight workout to my mornings, and this is what I did and didn't notice after 30 days. Why does micromovement matter? A post shared by Tom's Guide Fitness (@tomsguidefitness) A photo posted by The decision to stand rather than sit or to take the stairs over the escalator determines how much movement you fit into your day and how much energy you burn outside of workouts, also known as Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis, or NEAT. Just because you fit a 45-minute HIIT workout into your day doesn't undo the impact of accumulated sitting time, so how often you get up and move about really does matter for your long-term health. 7-minute micro-workout The movements below can help maintain functional strength, relieve stress, combat sedentary time, and move your muscles and joints, which increases oxygen-rich blood flow around the body. Here's the routine I followed every morning for 30 days. Future Future Future Future Shutterstock Shutterstock Squats: Squats build lower-body strength and help you maintain independence as you age. Strong legs and glutes contribute to activities like walking or running, and keep the hips, knees and ankles strong and mobile. Push-ups: Push-ups build strength in your triceps, shoulders and pecs while improving pushing power. Focus on maximal range of motion by extending your elbows, then lowering your chest as close to the floor as you can. Engage your core, and exhale as you press up. Cat-cow: Cat-cows improve spinal mobility and posture awareness and reduce stiffness. Try to increase your range of motion with every rep, inhaling as you drop your stomach and exhaling as you round through your spine. Shoulder blade squeezes: Squeezes strengthen the upper back and improve posture. This is also a great way to increase activity in the rear stabilizing muscles of the shoulders, which supports shoulder mechanics. Keep your shoulders relaxed. Lunges: Lunges are a unilateral strengthening exercise targeting the hips, glutes, hamstrings, quads and calves, improving balance and stability. Reversing your lunge puts less pressure on the knees; forward lunging improves quad emphasis. Sit-ups: Sit-ups strengthen the core, namely the rectus abdominis, which is a large superficial layer of muscles along the abdomen that works as you flex your torso. Focus on keeping your feet pressed into the ground and try to sit upright so that your hands can pass your toes. Supermans: This back exercise works the muscles along your posterior chain, including the upper, mid and lower back, glutes, hamstrings, plus your arms and shoulders. It's a great one to try if you don't have weights to row or pull. What happened when I tried it everyday for 30 days? (Image credit: Future) I love functional compound bodyweight exercises because they target the main muscle groups in your body and they can still feel challenging. If you're short on time and just want to get some movement in while you can, 60 seconds of each move performed back-to-back gives you a seven-minute full-body workout before you've even brushed your teeth in the morning. I love that I could work my chest, shoulders, arms, back, glutes, core and legs without picking up a single weight or worrying over getting to the gym. I hadn't fatigued myself enough that I couldn't then go to Pilates, the yoga studio, or out for a run later in the day, and I had woken up my muscles, oiled my joints and got fresh blood flow pumping around my body while lifting my heart rate. All before I had…

articles.title: I’m a professional video editor who just spent two weeks using the MacBook Pro OLED — and it’s such a huge upgrade from my older M1 Max that I can’t go back
articles.content: I preordered my 14-inch M1 Max MacBook Pro in October 2021, the week Apple announced it. It was my first Mac, and I documented the whole awkward leap in a video called "PC FanBoy Switches to NEW MacBook Pro - Should You?" . Learning macOS as a complete noob was painful for several weeks, and it didn't really click until a few months later. But when it finally did, I got why creators love these things. Five years later, it's the longest I've ever gone without "needing" a new laptop. It was one of my most expensive purchases at the time, but looking back all these years, probably one of the best investments I've ever made, despite how sad it made my bank statement look. Since joining the Tom's Guide video team, my DaVinci Resolve projects have become far more demanding, with easily 8+ layers and several heavy GPU effects running at once. That finally caught up with my 5-year-old M1 Max, which now wheezes like it just climbed 10 flights of stairs. Every new MacBook Pro since has looked appealing, and I won't lie, I've had a few Apple shopping carts configured, but I never found it in me to hit that checkout button. Then Apple announced the MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR Display , and three things caught my eye: a tandem OLED screen (two OLED layers stacked for more brightness), a lighter body, and a touchscreen. Touch was the big keynote moment, but everything else made me ready to upgrade. What 5 years of upgrades look like for me (Image credit: Tom's Guide) For the past two weeks, I've edited exclusively on the 16-inch MacBook Pro OLED in the M5 Max, 128GB, nano-texture configuration. Here's what the jump from my old 14-inch M1 Max with 32GB looks like. The chip goes from M1 Max to M5 Max, and the memory quadruples. The screen grows from 14 inches to 16. I've wished for that bigger screen for years, but I always talked myself out of a 16-inch because of the weight. This one weighs 4.1 pounds, about 0.6 pounds less than the previous 16-inch MacBook Pro. My M1 Max is around 3.5 pounds, so for roughly 0.6 pounds more I get a much bigger display. It's the first time a 16-inch laptop felt worth it to me. The new screen is a big part of why: it's what makes the body lighter, thinner, and slightly smaller, even though the display is slightly larger than on the non-touch MacBook Pros. At 0.63 inches thick, it's a hair slimmer than the 0.66-inch non-touch model; the footprint is slightly smaller, and the display grows from 16.2 to 16.3 inches. Then there are ports. My M1 Max has Thunderbolt 4, and that's why my massive Dell 52-inch 6K monitor was always stuck at 60Hz. The new laptop has three Thunderbolt 5 ports (the faster version of the same USB-C connector), and my monitor finally runs at 144Hz. Wi-Fi also jumps to Wi-Fi 7 from the Wi-Fi 6 on my old Mac, giving me faster connectivity when I'm working on the go. And don't forget the return of the glowing Apple logo on the lid. The last MacBook Pro with one was back in 2015, so I only ever admired it from the outside, like the cool kids' lunch table. Sure, I never actually saw it glow, but I'm finally sitting at the table. The screen is the real reason (Image credit: Tom's Guide) But here's what's really important. This is the best laptop display I've ever tested. I ran the same video project on this and a non-OLED MacBook Pro, and the shadows and bright scenes make fine details and color editing more precise. Apple rates the panel at up to 2,000 nits, and our lab measured 1,949, the brightest laptop screen Tom's Guide has tested. The nano-texture glass is one of the most important choices you'll make here. It's an anti-glare finish that costs $150 extra, and while Apple has offered it before, it's especially worth it on a touchscreen. The surface feels smoother and more premium under your finger, while the standard glass feels more resistant by comparison. It also hides fingerprints better. It's also why I can finally work away from my desk. I never used to edit on the go or outside…

articles.content: Watch Australia vs New Zealand in the Rugby League World Cup 2026 final from the Suncorp Stadium, Brisbane, as the tournament's two best men's teams meet again. The Kangaroos go for a 13th world crown, with the Kiwis looking to invoke the spirit of 2008 thanks to a returning great. Still unbeaten, Australia began to resemble their best version in the 44-12 semi-final victory over Samoa a week ago. A hat-trick from Reece Walsh did the damage, backing up Kevin Walters' call at leaving James Tedesco – captain of the 2026 premiers, no less – kicking his heels in reserve. Walsh's backflip after scoring one of his tries has brought a hope from his head coach to tone down the celebrations, while Walters has pulled another late surprise by promoting prop Keaon Koloamatangi to start just as he did against Samoa. The pack has been the Kangaroos Achilles' heel all tournament as they seek a 10th title from their past 11 attempts. James Tedesco has been added to interchange. Just 23 days after breaking his arm, Kalyn Ponga made a stunning return to start at fullback in beating a spirited Tonga 34-10 in the last four. Ponga lit up the opening-night 24-22 defeat by the Kangaroos and his convalescence will make his matchup with Walsh a spectacular prospect. Casey McLean scored his eighth try of the tournament – and 18th in eight Tests – to continue his burgeoning reputation and will again be a major worry for the 12-time world champions. In 2008, the Kiwis pulled off one of the sport's biggest upsets to win – 18 years on, Stacey Jones' side are much more an equal and quietly fancy their chances. articles.title: Did Alice Huang's Megaspeed Bypass America's Controls on Exporting Nvidia Chip to China?
articles.content: In three years "Megaspeed International" went from from inactive Chinese gaming subsidiary "to one of Asia's biggest buyers of cutting-edge semiconductors from the US," reports CNN. "It is incredibly hard to look at this and not see a Chinese state-sponsored network for bypassing US export control networks," trade data investigator William George told CNN. As Nvidia's Jensen Huang had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, "Megaspeed quietly instilled billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in data centers across Southeast Asia," CNN writes, noting scrutiny of the company from the Singapore government and US officials "concerned that the company was passing those chips on to unauthorized Chinese buyers..." In 2022, the US began restricting sales of semiconductors to China, including Nvidia's most advanced. While the controls were meant to curb China's tech industry, they also spawned opportunities for intermediaries willing to help circumvent them. US officials believe Megaspeed may be one of those... [T]rade records show Megaspeed has purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia... Based on indictments and investigative reports, research institute Epoch AI estimates that anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors were sent to China in violation of export controls last year... Singapore also initiated investigations into Megaspeed and its controllers, including Alice Huang, for potential false declarations relating to the company's server purchases and their final destinations. In a statement, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said there was insufficient evidence that Huang had committed any related offenses, but she had been barred from re-entering the country after providing inaccurate information "to downplay her role" at Megaspeed. The other investigations are ongoing. The exact scale of Chinese chip smuggling is impossible to quantify. However, its existence has become something of an open secret in the industry, as well as an indication that US efforts to keep adversaries from securing high-stakes technology still have fundamental flaws. A May report from the short seller Culper Research claimed that despite tightening trade restrictions, Chinese end-users still account for about 20% of Nvidia chip sales via illegal diversion and intermediaries in Southeast Asia. CNN reminds readers that Jensen Huang accompanied US President Trump to events with Chinese leader Xi Jinping twice this year, and also lobbied for the US to relax controls on Chinese chip imports. "The US government ultimately approved several buyers for less-advanced Nvidia chips, known as H200, while collecting a quarter of the revenue." "However, blacklisted companies have continued to obtain sensitive semiconductors as well," they add. And the Taiwanese government is even seeking to criminalize unauthorized exports of advanced AI chips to China, "as prosecutors there charged nine people in a scheme to sneak Nvidia chips into China through Japan, Indonesia and Hong Kong." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: 50th Anniversary of 'Star Wars' Celebrated with iMax 70mm Re-Release, Special Events, New Movie
articles.content: "Lucasfilm and Disney have restored the original Star Wars (1977) and will release the film in multiple formats, including Imax 70mm [starting February 19], as part of the franchise's 50th anniversary celebrations," reports Deadline. The original film will also be displayed in its original 16:9 format on the center of Cosm's 12K+ LED Dome, in a special presentation developed with Disney, Lucasfilm, ILM, and MakeMake. They're calling it a "Shared Reality production" where "the surrounding visual environments dynamically evolve to immerse the audience in iconic Star Wars locations and moments." Deadline reports more 50th anniversary celebrations In addition to the Imax 70mm screenings, the film will also be presented in Digital Imax, Digital Cinema, 70mm, 35mm, and 4DX. On May 4th, 2027, Lucasfilm will release a new behind-the-scenes documentary, The Hero Awakens, from filmmaker R.J. Cutler on Disney+. Star Wars events already on the calendar for 2027 include Shawn Levy's [movie] Star Wars: Starfighter, which will be released May 28. There's also a new poster paying homage to the original 1977 film, reports the Disney news site Mickey Visit, plus a newly orchestrated score by John Williams that they assume "will be used on all the projects that debut this year." On April 2-3, [Disney] will debut the new "Star Wars in Concert: The Skywalker Saga" at the Hollywood Bowl. The show will be hosted by Anthony Daniels, known for his role as C-3PO. Special performances of John Williams' iconic film scores will feature scenes and music from all nine Skywalker Saga films. The concert is a sweeping celebration of the stories, themes, and music that have inspired audiences around the world for five decades... They also teased that new and legacy licensees — including Hasbro, the LEGO Group, adidas, Mars, Aston Martin, Steinway, Hajime Sorayama presented by Complex, and more — will introduce 50th-anniversary collections... In the opening of the press release, Disney mentioned that as part of the announcements there will be "reimagined Disney Parks and Cruise Line offerings." The article adds that the April's Star Wars Celebration at the Los Angeles Convention Center has already sold out. There's more Star Wars news, writes long-time Slashdot reader schwit1 A light saber used by Darth Vader in the "Star Wars" movies The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi sold Thursday for nearly $5 million in an auction. The light saber, which was used in the climactic duel in Cloud City in which Vader tells Luke Skywalker "I am your father" sold for $4.875 million at the Ultimate Star Wars Auction held by Heritage Auctions. The sale marks a world auction record for any "Star Wars" collectible, according to the auction house. The previous record was Heritage's $3,750,000 sale of Luke Skywalker's lightsaber and severed hand effects rig on July 15, 2026. And they're still auctioning more Star Wars memorabilia... Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Rainbow Six Siege Year 11 Season 4 sees the return of a largely forgotten healer and a host of welcome changes to the UI and ranked ecosystem — here's everything you need to know
articles.content: If you tuned in to the Rainbow Six Siege Osaka majors this weekend, you’ll have noticed that a long-sidelined operator took center stage — Doc. As 20 teams duked it out in front of a screaming crowd, competing to earn $200,000 in prize money, the trophy they were coveting was shaped in the likeness of the healer-focused operator. As palpable tension rippled through the packed ATC hall, moments before the tournament’s final, we soon discovered why. A pre-Finals panel revealed that in Season 4, the largely forgotten healing character will be getting a huge revamp. Instead of shooting direct stim pistol darts from afar, Doc will now be armed with a brand new gadget — the E-HEAL Monitor system. Using the E-HEAL, Doc will be able to remotely heal and — even revive — teammates from across the map (including through walls). (Image credit: Ubisoft) It turns out, it's a good time to be a support player, because the Doc isn't the only healer-focused update coming next season. Operator Thunderbird is also coming back in a big way, with her Kóna Stations receiving a significant buff. Her number of Kóna Stations will be increased from 3 to 4 for broader site coverage, and if that wasn't enough to make you consider her, she’ll receive a new weapon too: the MBZ-19. Thunderbirds really are go. Alongside these intriguing operator remasters, an FPS legend is joining the fray — the Doom Slayer. In this surprise collaboration with Doom, the iconic anti-hero will become a part of Siege on December 22 in skin form — and you can read more about that here . A drastic UI overhaul (Image credit: Ubisoft) The beloved map Bank has also had an update that seeks to level the playing field between attackers and defenders. Adding a new access point and exterior cover around the entry point, Ubisoft Montreal says they're aiming to rebalance a map that's currently weighted too heavily in the defenders' favour. A new temporary testing ground will also allow the community to weigh in on a potential new secondary gadget which allows defenders to reinforce just part of a wall, leaving the rest open for lines of sight. Yet for hardcore fans, some of the most welcome changes will be the least exciting on paper. For year 11 and season 4, Rainbow Six Siege 's UI has undergone a drastic overhaul, and with it, new types of matchmaking have been introduced. The Ranked ecosystem is getting an overhaul, splitting the competitive mode into dedicated Ranked Solo/Duo and Ranked Flex playlists. The aim is to keep individual and duo players from clashing with larger, coordinated squads, hopefully saving some frustration and heartache for solo players. This will work in conjunction with Cross-Queue Matchmaking, in a bid to keep those match queue times fast. Additionally, the level requirement to unlock Ranked will be dropping from 50 to 30, helping newer players to jump in sooner. Ranked playlist alterations are finally here (Image credit: Ubisoft) “The solo/duo ranked playlist is something that we've been trying to do for years,” beams Rainbow Six Siege Game Director Chris Budgens, "We've always gotten cold feet, so we started looking at how we actually pull off a solo queue within Siege, while respecting healthy queue times and so on. Every time we tried to do it, we would get scared by the data — this might be a bit more destructive than we're ready to deal with at the moment because we had other known quantities such as Rank 3.0 we wanted to work on.” “We had so much data support in terms of our analysts and simulations and matchmaking queue times, and finally cracked it,” he adds. “We're really happy to be able to bring that to players because they've been asking for years to have a solo queue playlist.” Alongside new ranking queues, playing with your friends promises to be markedly less of a pain in the backside. An all-new Social Hub consolidates Ubisoft Connect and first-party platform friends into a single list, aiming to offer cleaner and less intrusive notifications.…

articles.title: 'You can't just take any IP character and throw them in because it just doesn't work. That's where skin collaborations work' — The Doom Slayer is the latest gaming icon to join Rainbow Six Siege and will be fragging his way onto Season 4
articles.content: Doom’s iconic anti-hero is ripping and tearing his way into Rainbow Six Siege. Taking to the stage in Osaka during Rainbow Six Siege ’s 2026 Majors tournament, Creative Director Joshua Mills revealed that the legendary first-person shooter (FPS) protagonist will be fragging his way into Siege as a new skin for Tachanka. Heading to the game on December 22, players will get a chance to rip and tear their way across the Siege universe as part of the game’s long-awaited fourth season. While the Doom Slayer’s in-game skin has yet to be revealed, his appearance was teased via a short video. As a portal to hell opens into the biker gang compound map Clubhouse, the Doom Slayer blasts a moving Rainbow Six drone before Mick Gordon’s signature guitar riff kicks in. The Doom Slayer skin comes after a wave of recent similar collaborations, with everything from Halo , Resident Evil , and Tomb Raider skins making appearances in Ubisoft’s FPS. “Doom means so much to me personally, and for many on the team that played Doom as kids growing up,” says Game Director Chris Budgens. “I think that skins are the best way [to implement most collaborations]. With skins, we get a lot more leeway in terms of having fun with the characters and franchises. To date, Rainbow Six Siege has only one permanent canon playable operator from a different fictional universe — Metal Gear Solid ’s Solid Snake — and as The Doom Slayer joins as a skin, it appears that Ubisoft Montreal wants to keep it that way for now. “We don't want to just flood the game with different partners,” reflects Budgens. “It has to be right.” Re-imagining icons (Image credit: Ubisoft) Snake’s inclusion, it seems, has been well judged. Since Solid Snake’s surprise introduction to Siege in March 2026, he’s become a beloved character in the game, slotting into Siege’s more grounded fictional universe with surprising ease. As I sit backstage at the Osaka 2026 majors, Ubisoft Montreal tells me that Solid Snake’s inclusion was an IP infiltration years in the making. “We had originally brought up the idea, and [Konami] were interested right from the get-go,” reveals Budgens. “One of the funny things was, what does this actually look like? Are we going with a skin? We had some interest in bringing Solid Snake as the operator into the game, but we had never really done that before—an operator from another franchise.” Creative director Joshua Mills, however, needed a bit more convincing that Snake would work in Siege’s gritty, grounded universe. “Alex Karpazis, the previous creative director, brought the idea to me and said, 'Listen, I want to bring [Snake] into the game, and I was like, 'You want to do what? How's that going to work?'” recalls Mills, “'If you say the cardboard box, I'm walking away right now!” In order to make Snake work alongside Sam Fisher and alongside SWAT team-esque operators, they decided to reimagine Snake as a Tom Clancy-esque agent. “We came up with a very clear rationale, which was: it's Solid Snake as if he existed within the Rainbow Six universe,” recalls Mills. “It allows us to take everything that's iconic about the character and make it more grounded and canon in Rainbow Six …. Then we got to make that legendary pairing with Snake and Zero [Sam Fisher], an opportunity of a lifetime to be able to do that.” Where the Doom Slayer is very much a classic skin-based collaboration, Mills suggests that The Boss’ inclusion in Rainbow Six Siege has opened the door to future fully fledged third-party operators. “We've definitely talked about other collaborations for a canon-based operator,” teases Mills. "We're very, very strict about who we would work with on this and who we would bring in because, again, we have to rationalise it one way or another. You can't just take any IP character and throw them in because it just doesn't work. That's where skin collaborations work fine… [but for operators ] There are some ideas, but nothing to confirm at the moment." You can read more…

articles.title: Bitcoin Plummets 24% in 46 Days as Crypto Falls on Rising Inflation
articles.content: October 3: $84,680 Today: $64,108 Bitcoin dropped 24.2% in 46 days. And it "fell more than 4% on Friday to $68,500," reports Fortune, "wiping out gains built over the past three months and casting doubt on whether its bear market was ever really over." The asset also faces weaker investor appetite, according to crypto analytics provider CryptoQuant. The firm's demand indicator recorded its weakest reading since December 2023, while Bitcoin exchange-traded funds became net sellers again. The recent downturn has also extended to other parts of the crypto market. That includes Tether's USDT, the largest cryptocurrency pegged to the U.S. dollar, whose total value shrank by $7.7 billion over the past two months, according to CryptoQuant, a sign that less cash is available in crypto markets. This time around, inflation has been the main culprit. Tuesday's Consumer Price Index report showed prices rose 0.4% in October, more than economists expected. Even stripping out food and energy, inflation ran hotter than forecast. Traders now overwhelmingly expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point in December, with some betting on an even bigger increase. "Because these are non-yielding assets, and we expect inflation to rise... people are chucking stuff like gold and Bitcoin to find... government bonds that are going up, providing you [with] income," Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at financial technology company IG Group, told Fortune... Heavy borrowing and spending on AI have created what 21Shares calls an "AI black hole," drawing money toward the sector and away from assets like Bitcoin and gold. But Bitcoin remains "joined at the hip" with tech stocks, according to Beauchamp. That leaves it in an awkward position: It faces competition for investment dollars when enthusiasm for AI runs high, yet can get dragged down when that enthusiasm fades. Fast Company points out Bitcoin "remains down more than 20% since the beginning of 2026." [Nvidia] has seen its shares lose more than 27% of their value over the past month. The tech sell-off seems to have dragged down the crypto markets, too, as the two sectors are, on some levels, intermingled... On top of that, outflows from Bitcoin funds may also be contributing to the slide. More than $1 billion in leveraged crypto positions were closed in recent days, which may have added to declining demand, affecting BTC prices. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: With Starship catch, SpaceX still shows it can dazzle the world
articles.content: STARBASE, Texas —The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position. Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms. Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket. Read full article Comments

articles.title: America Officially Loses Its Measles-elimination Status After Continued Spread of the Disease
articles.content: Reuters reports: The Pan American Health Organization has revoked the United States' measles-elimination status, ending a 26-year run after determining the country failed to halt continuous transmission of the highly contagious virus for more than a year, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday... The reported decision by the Americas branch of the World Health Organization comes as the US battles the highest number of measles cases it has seen in more than three decades. Some 7,500 people in the US have been infected with measles and 13 have died since 2025. That period coincides with falling immunization rates and rising vaccine hesitancy under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has for years spread doubts, without scientific evidence, about the safety of measles vaccines... Canada, Spain and the UK recently lost measles-elimination status after review by WHO experts.... "It is a fully preventable disease. It is unconscionable that we have this amount of measles," said Noel Brewer, a public health professor at the University of North Carolina... William Moss, an epidemiology professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, said loss of measles elimination was a hit to the United States' reputation as a public health powerhouse... For the average American, he added, it means that the United States will continue to have large outbreaks, putting people at risk of disease, hospitalization and death. articles.title: Manjaro Linux Moves Toward Independent Community Governance
articles.content: Arch-based Manjaro Linux "has announced that Manjaro Project e.V. is now officially registered as a non-profit in Germany," reports Linuxiac, "and is therefore a legally separate entity from the commercial Manjaro GmbH & Co. KG... after months of internal wrangling over who was in charge of the project, who had access to the infrastructure and who didn't, and the relationship between the dev team and the commercial company..." The restructuring goes back to March, when the Manjaro developers released the Manjaro 2.0 Manifesto, which was a very public critique of the way Manjaro was being run. The document claims that decision-making has effectively become the sole domain of the project founder, Philip Müller, with the other developers having very limited access to the infrastructure. There's also a concern about the drop in participation, the persistent technical issues, and the continued prioritization of commercial interests over the actual development of the distribution... The manifesto proposed the transfer of all project infrastructure, domains, repositories and community funds to the new organization, together with arrangements for the use of the Manjaro trademark. The contributors were warning that they might well consider forking the distro if the talks didn't go their way. Müller then indicated that he'd be happy to talk about the proposed structure once the non-profit was in place. The association is now formally registered, and so one of the key aims of the manifesto has been realized... Perhaps the most important point is the actual evolution of the distribution. The most recent testing and stable updates were kicked off by the Manjaro team themselves, without any oversight from Müller. This points to the developers having already started to operate on their own in an area which was previously the preserve of the project's founder. They're also in the process of optimizing their dev infrastructure, in part as a response to the continued automated bot attacks on the existing infrastructure. Thanks to Slashdot reader king*jojo for sharing the news. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Who should run Nvidia? Our picks for Jensen Huang’s successor, whether the board likes it or not
articles.content: Jensen Huang, top left, and 11 executives mentioned in this story as possible successors. Top row, from left: Huang, Rene Haas, Colette Kress and Ian Buck. Middle: Lisa Su, Thomas Kurian, Peter DeSantis and Dave Treadwell. Bottom: Amy Hood, Matt Garman, Judson Althoff and Nick Parker. (Company and LinkedIn Photos) Nvidia’s board says it’s too early to speculate about who will succeed Jensen Huang. Sorry, we’re having too much fun coming up with names. The board said in a statement Friday that it’s still choosing a search firm and hasn’t formally engaged any candidates. That came after the Financial Times reported that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas — a name John had presciently floated when we recorded this week’s GeekWire Podcast on Thursday. Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy. Colette Kress , the company’s longtime CFO, is serving as interim CEO. She spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career. Others would rather have Huang back. Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to run a deliberate search that leaves open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Elon Musk said on X that he was signing a petition to reinstate Huang. The organizers of one, called “ Stand with Jensen ,” say it has more than 108,000 names, including more than 5,600 people who identify themselves as current Nvidia employees. The case for Haas: The Arm CEO spent about seven years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in February 2022, when Nvidia’s $40 billion deal to acquire Arm collapsed amid regulatory opposition. SoftBank, Arm’s majority owner, kept Nvidia’s $1.25 billion prepayment. Arm, based in Cambridge, England, designs processor technology that’s ubiquitous in smartphones, and licenses it to other chipmakers. That includes Nvidia, whose Grace data center CPU , paired with its GPUs in AI systems, is built on Arm cores. Amazon’s Graviton and Microsoft’s Cobalt server chips also use Arm designs. Haas is one of several candidates, and there’s no guarantee he’ll be offered the job or take it, the FT reported. He also has a link to Harvey Jones, the longtime Nvidia director named the company’s first board chair this week. Haas was vice president of sales at Tensilica, a chip-design company, from 1999 to 2004, according to his LinkedIn profile. Jones co-founded Tensilica and chaired its board until chip-design software maker Cadence acquired it in 2013. Haas has also seen Huang’s resistance to succession planning firsthand. “He didn’t like the idea,” Haas said in a 2024 interview, as quoted by the New York Times this week. “He felt it would create competition among executives and be divisive.” One complication: SoftBank named Haas CEO of SoftBank Group International in April, helping coordinate chip and AI companies in its international portfolio while he continues to run Arm. The FT reported that the appointment was aimed at pushing forward Project Izanagi , SoftBank’s AI chip effort launched to compete with Nvidia. He knows Nvidia from the inside, but he also knows what it’s like to run a public company — which matters for a board searching in the middle of a crisis. John’s argument on the podcast: Nvidia needs someone who can shepherd a company through turmoil, not just a great technologist. Think Alan Mulally going from Boeing to Ford, or Dara Khosrowshahi moving from Expedia to Uber after Travis Kalanick’s…

articles.title: EFF Criticizes US Government's Use of AI For Evaluating Senior Health Insurance Requests
articles.content: "When we need medical care, we expect decisions about our treatment to be made by our doctors, not a tech company's algorithm," writes the EFF newsletter EFFector. But in January America's federal government launched a program called WISeR that uses AI to evaluate authorization requests for certain procedures from America's federal health insurance program for seniors, Medicare. EFF sued for records and discovered "additional issues" with the program that they say "could jeopardize Medicare beneficiaries' access to care." The records we received revealed that WISeR has resulted in widespread delays and denials of care, operational chaos, and reports of patient harm. Further documents obtained by EFF show a rushed and rocky rollout, highlighting the dangers that arise when governments treat AI like a silver bullet for complex problems. EFF has now published hundreds of pages of documents obtained through our lawsuit, available here... The documents also highlight the need for more transparency about safeguards against inappropriate, AI-driven denials. EFF has long argued that AI has no place in consequential government decisions about peoples' rights or access to benefits, such as immigration enforcement and policing decisions. That's because using automated decision-making in these contexts risks decisions that violate people's rights or deprive them of benefits they're entitled to based on biased or inappropriate considerations and without proper due process or accountability if there is an error. By outsourcing decision-making to private AI companies without sufficient transparency, testing, or legal limits, WISeR jeopardizes seniors' access to medical care. Congress should step in to place greater legal limits on the use of automated decision-making in Medicare. The new documents "show why we need stronger legal limits around government use of automated decision-making..." according to the newsletter. And another EFF page argues that the American public "still lacks the information needed to assess whether clinician review is providing meaningful oversight of AI systems and whether appropriate data is being used to evaluate prior authorization requests." WISeR's payment structure gives vendors, as the government put it, "an incentive to deny as many claims as possible...." [One company] denied more requests than it approved in the first few months of the program, and CMS inquired about "denials that appear inaccurate or inconsistent with applicable criteria." Ultimately, the records obtained by EFF raise more questions than they answer about the safeguards used by WISeR vendors... A growing body of scholarship points to the substantial limitations of "human in the loop" policies as guardrails for AI systems. AI-generated recommendations can unduly influence human decisions, leading reviewers to over-rely on automated judgements and rubber stamp them as correct. Even worse, at least one health insurance company actively pressured clinical reviewers to accept its AI systems' recommendations. Another company built a system that allowed clinical reviewers to reject claims without opening patient files; clinical reviewers using this system spent an average of just 1.2 seconds on each case.. As the government expands its use of automated decision-making, the potential for consequential mistakes increases rapidly. The records we've obtained so far raise questions about the rushed rollout and lack of guardrails for automated decision-making by the U.S. government. EFF urges transparency, oversight, and legal limits to protect people from the harms of automated decision-making in high risk systems. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Hundreds of Fake Accounts Defended Jensen Huang On Social Media
articles.content: The Washington Post reports on something peculiar about support for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang online after he'd told the world he'd been unfaithful to his wife (before reports of his second extramarital affair): Joining the chorus online were voices of seemingly everyday people: a chef, a stock trader, a Hebrew teacher and several environmental activists. But at least 400 of them were fake, according to research from the nonprofit Midas Project, with links to a public relations firm involved in previous so-called "sockpuppet" campaigns... Many of the fake accounts, according to Midas Project executive director Tyler Johnston, replied to journalists, former U.S. officials and other prominent figures and backed not just Huang but Nvidia's push to sell its cutting-edge chips to Chinese firms. Like other documented influence campaigns, the posts appeared to have limited reach; the most-viewed tweet garnered about 8,000 views and 32 likes. Still, some of the posts targeted lawmakers, including accounts for the [U.S.] House Select Committee on China, Republicans on the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts). "That's a place where you might not need a lot of views, but maybe the staffers who are running the lawmakers' account are paying attention to how their messages are received," said Johnston, whose group advocates for safe AI development... There were other clues that helped identify accounts as being part of an apparently coordinated campaign, according to the Midas Project. Some of them were created minutes or hours apart, and had user names and profile photos refreshed at similar times. They also sometimes engaged on oddly specific issues ranging from Qatar to Nippon Steel's bid for U.S. Steel and a waste management plant in Oregon.... Any one one of the posts — often replies to other posts — might have not looked suspicious in isolation. But the various clues taken together, Johnston said, gave evidence that they were linked. Some of the accounts then rushed to delete posts after he posted his findings online, and at least 260 of them have been deactivated or suspended by X. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Why Your NumPy Array Changed After Preprocessing (Views vs Copies in ML)
articles.content: A small NumPy operation can modify data you never intended to touch. Understanding views, copies, and memory sharing can prevent silent bugs in machine learning pipelines. Introduction Imagine preparing a dataset for a machine learning model. You load the original data, select a few columns, normalize their values, and pass the result to your training algorithm. Everything appears to work correctly. Later, when you inspect the original dataset, something looks wrong. Some values have changed, even though you never directly modified the original array. This is one of those Python behaviors that can make debugging surprisingly difficult. The problem usually comes down to how NumPy handles memory. When you create a new array from an existing one, NumPy does not always allocate new memory. Sometimes, it creates a view that points to the same underlying data. This matters most during preprocessing, where slicing, normalization, reshaping, and feature selection are common. Let’s look at why it happens, how to detect it, and how to avoid it. 1. The Difference Between a NumPy View and a Copy A view creates a new array object that shares memory with another array. A copy creates a separate array with its own data. import numpy as np original = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50]) view = original[1:4] view[0] = 999 print("Original:", original) print("View:", view) Output: Original: [ 10 999 30 40 50] View: [999 30 40] The original array changed even though we modified only the view variable. Basic slicing creates a view, so both arrays reference the same memory for the selected elements. Now, the same operation with .copy() : original = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50]) copied = original[1:4].copy() copied[0] = 999 print("Original:", original) print("Copy:", copied) Output: Original: [10 20 30 40 50] Copy: [999 30 40] The original array is unchanged. The difference isn’t in the variable names or values. It’s in how NumPy manages memory. If you’ve seen the same idea with plain Python lists, see Why .copy() in Python Still Mutates Your Original List. 2. Why This Becomes a Problem During ML Preprocessing Machine learning preprocessing often involves selecting features and transforming numerical values. import numpy as np data = np.array([ [100, 20, 5], [200, 30, 10], [300, 40, 15], [400, 50, 20] ], dtype=float) Suppose the first two columns are features you want to center around zero. A developer might write: features = data[:, :2] features -= features.mean(axis=0) print(features) print(data) The features look correct: [[ -150. -15.] [ -50. -5.] [ 50. 5.] [ 150. 15.]] But the original dataset has also changed: [[-150. -15. 5.] [ -50. -5. 10.] [ 50. 5. 15.] [ 150. 15. 20.]] The cause is this line: features = data[:, :2] Slicing created a view of data . Then features -= ... modified the values in place, and since features and data share memory, the change appeared in both. This is especially dangerous when the original dataset is needed for another preprocessing step, a model comparison, or evaluation. 3. The Fix: Create an Independent Copy Before Preprocessing Instead of: features = data[:, :2] use: features = data[:, :2].copy() features -= features.mean(axis=0) print("Processed features:") print(features) print("Original dataset:") print(data) The processed features are transformed, and the original dataset stays intact. This .copy() call makes the intent explicit: the preprocessing should work on independent data. Copying everything is not always necessary, though, because it increases memory usage, especially with large datasets. The better habit is knowing when NumPy shares memory and when it doesn’t. 4. How to Check Whether Two Arrays Share Memory NumPy provides np.shares_memory() for this: import numpy as np original = np.arange(10) view = original[2:7] copied = original[2:7].copy() print(np.shares_memory(original, view)) print(np.shares_memory(original, copied)) Output: True False You can also inspect the .base attribute: print(view.base is…

articles.title: ‘I hope this email finds you’: Microsoft declares outage over as the world digs out of its inbox
articles.content: Microsoft says it has restored service after a Microsoft 365 outage cut off email in more than 70 countries. (GeekWire File Photo / Todd Bishop) Steven Sinofsky was relieved this week to finally give up a title he never wanted. “Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group. Later in the day, he aired a pet peeve. After a plumber emailed to say he’d missed an appointment because of the “Outlook outage,” Sinofsky noted that this one wasn’t really the application’s fault. “This time it is the data center layer,” he wrote . Microsoft’s explanation backs him up. The company says the failure, which cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries this week, was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade in its Microsoft 365 cloud and surfaced after a more recent network change. It hasn’t given more details. Related ‘A huge pain in the ass’: Microsoft 365 starts to recover after a day of global email turmoil The company said late Friday it had restored service to the remaining customers and regions. The disruption lasted about 30 hours, according to Microsoft’s incident log . Microsoft offered a public apology and promised a detailed post-mortem explaining what went wrong and next steps. Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X Friday afternoon that “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” made recovery more difficult than normal. A “thundering herd” isn’t a stampede of frustrated IT admins descending on Redmond, as fitting as that might have been. It happens when huge numbers of devices try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online. He said the post-mortem would come “shortly,” with a “step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future.” In a reply to another user , he said Microsoft “will be very specific on what happened.” In its notice to customers, Microsoft said it would provide a preliminary post-incident report within two business days and a final report within five. In the meantime, like prior incidents involving AWS and others, the “Outlook outage” became the latest example of how much depends on one company’s cloud. Microsoft reported in January that it had more than 450 million paid commercial Microsoft 365 seats, roughly one for every 18 people on Earth. Among those affected this week were Unity Health Toronto , a hospital network that had to declare a Code Grey, the alert for a systems failure; a Colorado jail that couldn’t take online bond payments ; and Pennsylvania lawmakers who went about 18 hours without email. Unity Health said patient care continued without disruption. In Japan, securities firms and asset managers fell back on fax machines when trade-confirmation emails stopped coming through, Business Upturn reported , citing Nikkei. In New York, the city’s Emergency Management office warned of delays reaching city agencies. In Singapore, the outage disrupted some government systems , including email, and in London, the UK Supreme Court wasn’t receiving email. About the only thing that wasn’t Microsoft’s fault was Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Federal officials blamed aging FAA telecom gear . Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened an evening news conference — before even getting to the news that U.S. airspace had reopened — by saying there was “no connection between this and Microsoft,” adding, “I know a lot of people are making that jump.” Microsoft itself looked…

articles.title: My Local AI Agent Needed a Bigger Brain, So I Gave It a Decentralized GPU
articles.content: this is my second progress update for the Decentralize AI Hackathon by HackerNoon and Nosana. In my first article, I Built a Local AI Linux Assistant That Doesn't Rely on the Cloud , I introduced zkzkAgent: an AI agent that manages a Linux machine through plain language and runs entirely on my own hardware with Ollama. That is still how it works by default. But running everything locally has a ceiling, and I kept hitting it. The Problem: The Model That Fits on a Laptop zkzkAgent doesn't push every request through one big prompt. A small classifier node first decides what kind of request it is: a question to answer, a single action to run, or a task that needs a plan. Plans are where the agent is most useful, and they are also where the model works hardest. To scaffold a project, the planner writes every step, including the full content of every file, before anything runs. On my laptop, I run a 2B model ( qwen3.5:2b ). It fits in memory and answers quickly. A 27B model does not fit. Until now, anyone on modest hardware had two options: accept a small model, or send everything to a centralized AI provider. Nosana adds a third option: rent a GPU from a decentralized network, only for the model, and keep everything else at home. zkzkAgent in 30 Seconds A multi-node LangGraph graph . Separate nodes classify the request, answer questions, write plans, and execute tools. The router logs every decision with the reason for it. 25 tools for files, apps, networking, processes, packages, and deployment. Human-in-the-loop safety . Destructive tools (removing files, emptying the trash, installing or removing packages) are blocked in code until I type yes . A chat CLI with live streaming, history and slash commands, plus Docker support and an optional voice mode. The Design Rule: Only the Model Moves Before writing any code, I set one rule for the integration: Nosana gets the model calls and nothing else. The graph, the routing, the confirmation gates, and all 25 tools still run on my machine. A model on a remote GPU can suggest remove_file . Only my machine can run it, and only after I type yes . That rule kept the change small. It lives in one file, models/LLM.py , and it is controlled by one setting in `.env`: MODEL_TYPE="NOSANA" NOSANA_API_KEY="nos_..." NOSANA_BASE_URL="https://inference.nosana.com/v1" NOSANA_MODEL="qwen/qwen3.8-27b" Nosana's inference API uses the OpenAI chat format, so the agent talks to it through LangChain's `ChatOpenAI` client. The rest of the graph only sees an `llm` object and doesn't know which backend is behind it: if MODEL_TYPE == "NOSANA": API_KEY = _env("NOSANA_API_KEY") if not API_KEY.startswith("nos_"): raise RuntimeError("NOSANA_API_KEY missing or invalid (must start with 'nos_').") BASE_URL = _env("NOSANA_BASE_URL", NOSANA_URL).rstrip("/") MODEL_NAME = _env("NOSANA_MODEL") or _pick_nosana_model(BASE_URL, API_KEY) llm = ChatOpenAI( model=MODEL_NAME, base_url=BASE_URL, api_key=API_KEY, timeout=120, max_retries=2, stream_usage=True, # final chunk carries token counts ) elif MODEL_TYPE == "OLLAMA": pass #the other implement of the code Three details are worth explaining: Picking a live model. On Nosana, a model only appears in GET /models while a GPU is actually serving it. If `NOSANA_MODEL` is empty, the agent fetches that list and uses the first available model, so it never starts against a model that nobody is serving. Token counts . With stream_usage=True , the last streamed chunk includes token usage. That is what usage is billed on, and it is the basis for the cost numbers I plan to publish next. Bring your own GPU job. The repo also includes nosana-ollama.json , a Nosana job definition that starts the official Ollama container on a GPU node and pulls qwen3:14b . It is for people who want their own model server on Nosana instead of the shared API. articles.title: AWS Emulator proves agents need a verification loop. Realism is the hard part.
articles.content: This week, Amazon Web Services released AWS Emulator, a local copy of AWS that coding agents can test against. It covers more than 200 AWS services and was written entirely by agents. The most useful part of the launch is a story Swami Sivasubramanian tells in the announcement. About 20 years ago, Sivasubramanian helped build the replication engine inside Alf, a Paxos-based lock service that still powers AWS systems such as S3 and DynamoDB. The first build took about four months. When he later asked Kiro, AWS’s agentic coding tool, to rebuild it, he supervised the agent for four nights before he saw the problem: The agent had no way to check its own results. Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours. Same agent, same task. Four nights became two hours because the feedback loop changed. “An agent is only as good as its verification loop, and a verification loop is only as good as what it runs against.” As Sivasubramanian puts it, distributed systems are hard to test. That matches what I see across teams running coding agents on production systems. An agent is only as good as its verification loop, and a verification loop is only as good as what it runs against. AWS Emulator solves that for the AWS APIs your code calls. It does not solve it for the services your team owns, and that is where most agent-written changes break. AWS puts infrastructure inside the agent’s loop A coding agent works in a loop. It writes code, runs it, reads the result, and decides what to change next. Sivasubramanian’s point is that in distributed systems, that loop runs inside infrastructure. If the services the code calls do not behave like the real ones, the agent learns the wrong lesson and keeps going. AWS Emulator puts AWS into that loop on a laptop. Point existing AWS tools and code at it with one environment variable, and tests run against emulated services without changes. Autonomous agents wrote every line of the emulator, working from AWS’s public API models. Each behavior is pinned by a fidelity test that first passes against real AWS, then against the emulator, and every change passes a merge gate where security agents review it. Sivasubramanian’s conclusion is that when agents write the code, the engineer’s job is to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when the work is correct. The first reactions on Hacker News went straight to trust. One commenter counted roughly 30,000 commits in three weeks and questioned the quality. That is a fair question aimed at the wrong thing. Who wrote the code tells you little. What it was verified against tells you a lot, and AWS’s answer is real AWS. “Slow or unrealistic feedback was a tax on people. For agents, it decides whether the loop works at all.” What changed is who runs the loop. A developer checks a change a few times a day, and an agent checks it on every iteration. Slow or unrealistic feedback was a tax on people. For agents, it decides whether the loop works at all. Every loop runs against mocks, an emulator, or the running system An agent can verify its work against one of three things, and each has a different weakness. Mocks are the weakest option, and AI has made them cheap. One Hacker News commenter argued that it is now faster to have AI mock your APIs , adding that “AI has been a boon for test coverage.” But an agent that writes its own mocks writes them to match its own assumptions. The tests pass because they were built to pass, so coverage goes up while confidence should not. Emulators are a real step up. AWS Emulator is checked against real AWS, so its behavior comes from the service rather than from the agent. An emulator is still a model, though, and AWS is open about that. The repository keeps a folder of behaviors the agents found that do not match real AWS yet, and operations that are not implemented return an error instead of a fake success. An IDC…
