articles.title: How to Watch the Hunger Games Movies in Chronological Order
articles.content: So, full disclosure, I don’t really believe in watching movies in chronological order the first time around. I think that watching them by release date is usually the best way to go. However, if you’re planning on doing it for the Hunger Games movies, I’ve got you covered. Here are all the Hunger Games movies in chronological order. Hunger Games Movies in Chronological Order The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping The Hunger Games The Hunger Games: Catching Fire The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 1 The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 2 1. The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes The first movie in the Hunger Games’ timeline, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes sees a young Coriolanus Snow trying to navigate the craziness that is the country of Panem. He eventually finds himself actively involved in the 10th annual Hunger Games as a mentor for District 12’s female tribute, Lucy Gray Baird. Snow wants to be on top of the world, which means he’ll do anything and everything to see his dream realized. Cheat, kill, backstab - nothing is off limits if it means inching closer and closer to the top. 2. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping Set 40 years after the events of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, it focuses on District 12 male tribute Haymitch Abernathy as he is forced to compete in the 50th Hunger Games. This time, though, the rules have changed. Every 25th Hunger Games, a new concept is added to make that year’s game even more special. So, for the 50th Hunger Games, they decide to double the number of tributes. 48 in total, 4 from each district. It’s hard enough to win a normal Hunger Games, but to do it with double the people is damn near impossible. Haymitch will have to overcome the overwhelming odds if he wants to survive. 3. The Hunger Games Fast forward 24 years, and we arrive at the 74th Hunger Games. Yes, the Hunger Games are still going, but the 12 Districts that are forced to send their children to death every year are sick and tired of it all. Revolution is coming. All it needs is for someone to light the fire. In the midst of all this, District 12 teenager Katniss Everdeen volunteers to participate in the Hunger Games in place of her little sister. Alongside District 12 male tribute Peeta Mellark, Katniss will have to train and learn the inner workings of the games to outlast the other tributes and make it back home to her family. 4. The Hunger Games: Catching Fire The fire of rebellion is spreading, and the government of Panem knows that it has to do something before it spreads too far. Katniss, who survived last year’s games, is seen as a dangerous individual who’s fanning the flames. President Snow decides that something has to be done about her and the other former Hunger Games victors. For the 75th Hunger Games, a new special concept is added. Katniss and 23 other former Hunger Games winners will return to compete to the death. Knowing that they’re beloved by the populace, they tug at their heartstrings to try and get out of the games, further pushing people to revolt. 5. The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 1 The rebellion is in full swing following the games, and Katniss, whether she wants to or not, is seen as the face of it. Most of the districts are quick to join her side, but President Snow won’t go quietly into that good night. He still has a few tricks up his sleeve, including brainwashing someone who’s very close to Katniss. I can’t go into more detail without spoiling the movie, but this is where things get serious. And they only get more serious in the following and final movie. 6. The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 2 The war between the rebellion and President Snow is finally coming to an end. All the districts are united against him; the only thing left to do is to storm the Capitol and to take down the president himself. But President Snow refuses to lose gracefully. Throughout the city, he has laid out traps for Katniss…

articles.title: How to Evaluate Snowflake Cortex Embedding Models for Enterprise Search
articles.content: Picture this. A company has 500,000 support tickets sitting in Snowflake. Years of troubleshooting notes, product defects, workarounds, resolutions, and occasional messages that just say "fixed after restart." Very helpful, thanks. Someone wants an AI assistant that can search those tickets and suggest resolutions. The architecture looks straightforward. Take the documents, generate embeddings, store vectors, retrieve similar records, and let an LLM write the answer. A few SQL queries later, you have a demo. Then someone asks which embedding model you picked. "Arctic." Which Arctic? "The bigger one." Why? "More dimensions." And there it is. We've designed an intelligent search system using the same decision-making process people use to buy televisions. Snowflake Cortex offers eight built-in text embedding models through AI_EMBED . Some produce 768-dimensional vectors, others 1,024. Some are English-focused. Others support multiple languages. Context windows vary considerably. The problem isn't a shortage of options. It's figuring out what actually matters. I've spent about eight years working with Snowflake, and one lesson from enterprise data engineering keeps showing up: the technically impressive option isn't necessarily the right one for your workload. Embedding models are no exception. Meet the suspects According to Snowflake's AI_EMBED documentation, the built-in text embedding lineup includes: Model Dimensions Language focus snowflake-arctic-embed-m 768 English snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v1.5 768 English e5-base-v2 768 English snowflake-arctic-embed-l-v2.0 1,024 Multilingual snowflake-arctic-embed-l-v2.0-8k 1,024 Multilingual nv-embed-qa-4 1,024 English multilingual-e5-large 1,024 Multilingual voyage-multilingual-2 1,024 Multilingual Snowflake also supports image embeddings through voyage-multimodal-3 , but that's a different use case. We're keeping this investigation focused on text. Eight models sound like eight chances to get it right. Or eight chances to explain to your architect why you chose one based on a name. Let's narrow down the questions. Round 1: 1,024 dimensions versus 768 The first temptation is obvious. A 1,024-dimensional embedding contains more numbers than a 768-dimensional embedding. More numbers must mean more meaning. Unfortunately, vector search doesn't work like upgrading a laptop from 16 GB to 32 GB of RAM. An embedding model learns a representation of language. Its dimensions are coordinates in that learned space, not a score for intelligence. A larger representation might capture useful distinctions. It might also deliver no measurable improvement on your particular documents. Imagine three fictional incident records: Incident A: Payment reconciliation failed after an upstream schema change. Incident B: Settlement processing rejected records following a column modification. Incident C: The finance department completed its quarterly budget review. Now a user asks: "Why did settlement reconciliation fail after the column changed?" A useful model should recognize that A and B are relevant, while C is mostly unrelated. But here's the interesting part. Suppose a 768-dimensional model puts B first, while a 1,024-dimensional model puts A first. Which one won? You can't answer that from the dimension count. Maybe both are valid. Maybe one describes the exact failure while the other concerns an older version of the pipeline. Maybe neither contains the accepted resolution. The model's job isn't to produce a beautiful vector. It's to retrieve useful evidence. For an English-only knowledge base containing relatively short documents, I'd start with a compact model such as Arctic Embed M v1.5 as a baseline. Then I'd test whether a larger model improves retrieval. Not assume it does. Round 2: The multilingual trap Now the support organization expands. Some tickets are in English. Others are in Spanish, French, Japanese, or a combination of languages. One customer writes: "El proceso de conciliación falló…

articles.title: Windows 0-Day Dropped By Disgruntled Researcher Hands Hackers System Rights
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a "general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode." By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. [...] Researcher Will Dormann said in an interview that he has been able to reproduce the exploit and that it works as described, but not on all versions of Windows 11. But there's a catch, he said. "The requirements are important in that it seems to require Windows 26H2, and one that has existed for more than 90 days, it seems," he explained. "That is, you can't just take a new 26H2 system and install updates and have it work." For a system to be vulnerable, Dormann said, the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode value must be 0 or 1." Of the many machines Dormann uses, only a single one met this requirement. Microsoft said in a statement that it was investigating the vulnerability and had no evidence it was being exploited in the wild. The company also said Defender blocks potential exploitation attempts. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: FAA Lifts Nationwide Ground Stop for All Aircraft [UPDATE]
articles.content: Longtime Slashdot readers cold fjord and sinij share news that the FAA grounded flights nationwide after a communications failure disrupted air traffic control centers across the country. By Friday evening, the outage had resulted in nearly 5,000 flight cancellations and roughly 10,000 delays, with no timeline for restoring normal operations. Rumors are swirling that this could be related to the FAA's newly deployed SMART AI system or Microsoft's recent global outage, but both the agency and Microsoft said they had no indication that their technology was responsible. Business Insider reports: US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said just after 4:15 pm. Eastern time that the nationwide flight traffic halt came "following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." "FAA technicians are investigating the issue," he said in a post on X. The outage comes the same week as the FAA deployed SMART, a new AI tool to help air traffic control. ASI, the company that makes the SMART system for the FAA, said that Friday's issues weren't "based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC." Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a press conference Friday, when asked if the AI system might be related to the outage: "That's what we're looking at." Microsoft, which faced massive issues across its services this week, also said that it had "no indication" the ground stop was related to any Microsoft services. Meanwhile, the FAA said that the ground stop was due to "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." UPDATE 1:33 UTC: Secretary Mullin and Secretary Duffy are currently briefing members of the press on the issue. UPDATE 1:46 UTC: The FAA has lifted the nationwide ground stop after more than four hours. Officials said the disruption appears to have stemmed from a network router issue that cascaded nationwide, with no evidence of a cyberattack or connection to Microsoft's recent outage. Airlines warned that disruptions could continue in Saturday. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: How AI Agents Shape Human Judgment Through Analytical Assumptions
articles.content: A founder asks an AI agent to recommend which customer accounts deserve more attention. The agent checks revenue, support costs and renewal dates, then returns a sensible ranking. The numbers are accurate. The founder reviews the list and approves it. But somewhere along the way, the agent decided what “deserve more attention” meant. Perhaps it prioritised immediate revenue over customers with growth potential. Perhaps it treated support requests as costs rather than evidence that a customer needed help. The founder checked the answer. The objective behind it received less attention. This is a harder problem than catching a hallucination. Nothing needs to be false for a recommendation to carry a choice that the person receiving it never consciously made. When the calculation works Anthropic published research on 27 October examining how agents influence experts’ judgement calls. Fifty professional analysts used Claude Code to assess a farming advisory programme. Researchers secretly assigned each agent a preference between defensible analytical options, including how to measure productivity. Across four analytical choices, participants followed their agent’s assigned preference 86% of the time. The agents were instructed to make an honest case, not to deceive. The limits matter. This was one task, in one field, with deliberately strengthened agent preferences. It does not establish how often the same thing happens inside companies. It does show why checking whether an analysis is technically sound may leave an important question unanswered: who selected the assumptions that made this answer persuasive? An agent can help us reason while also steering what we consider reasonable. The decision inside the metric Consider a company asking AI to identify employees at risk of leaving. Before anyone discusses the accuracy of the predictions, several choices have already entered the task. Is every departure something the company wants to prevent? Should attention go to people whose replacement would be expensive, people with scarce capabilities, or people whose development has stalled? What happens when the best next step for an employee is outside the organisation? Different answers could produce different recommendations from the same information. None can be settled simply by making the model more accurate. For me, this is where conversations about human capability become practical. We ask people to exercise judgement, but then present them with a finished recommendation in which the most consequential choices have already been made. A manager might carefully inspect the evidence for contacting one employee without ever questioning why another employee was excluded from consideration. Their review can be diligent and still begin too late. Make the alternatives visible Before running a consequential analysis, the person responsible should write down what they want to achieve and what they are unwilling to sacrifice. It can be a short paragraph. The value comes from making the choice explicit enough to question. For the customer example, that might mean preserving long-term relationships while reducing avoidable support work. That instruction would lead to different questions from simply asking which accounts are most profitable. The agent can then help identify reasonable alternatives. What changes if we prioritise growth potential? Which customers move down the list if service costs carry more weight? What evidence would justify choosing one approach over another? Suppose both approaches produce accurate forecasts. One favours an established customer with predictable revenue; the other favours a smaller account that requires investment. The useful conversation is about the company's commercial priorities and obligations. Asking the agent to check its arithmetic again will not resolve that choice. This makes the disagreement available for discussion. A polished recommendation alone can conceal it. The same principle belongs in the…

articles.title: SpaceX Falls Short of Historic Double Starship Catch
articles.content: SpaceX's 15th Starship test flight successfully reached orbit Friday, but its historic attempt to catch both stages at the launch tower was derailed when the Super Heavy booster malfunctioned, forcing controllers to abort its return before it exploded after splashing down in the Gulf of Mexico. The upper-stage Starship did, however, successfully deploy 26 Starlink satellites and is scheduled to complete 15 orbits before attempting an unprecedented tower catch on Saturday. If successful, it would mark the first time a spacecraft has returned from orbit to land vertically at a launch tower. The Bakersfield Californian reports: The original goal was to retrieve every single piece of the rocket for the purpose of future recycling, something yet to be achieved anywhere in the world. Musk sees this leading to the kind of fast and consistent launch rates necessary for building moon bases and sending people to Mars. Shortly after reaching orbit, Starship dropped off 26 of the company's most advanced Starlink satellites. The plan is for Starship to complete 15 laps around the world at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) before heading back to the launch site for Saturday's grand finale. SpaceX had already made three booster grabs at the company's sprawling Starbase near the U.S.-Mexico border. That made Friday's miss all the more surprising. "Well, that certainly isn't the news that we had hoped to hear for today," observed SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice, adding that it was in line with the many rigorous safety checks to protect the pad. No explanation was provided for what went wrong. This was the first attempt to capture the upgraded version of the booster that stretches 236 feet (72 meters) -- the production model for moon and Mars expeditions. It will also be the first time the company attempts to catch the spacecraft, which spans 171 feet (52 meters). Together, they form the world's biggest and most powerful rocket -- an astounding 407 feet (124 meters) in height. The spacecraft portion of the 14 previous Starships ended up in the ocean, either by design at flight's end or by accident in a stream of flaming wreckage. During the first full-scale test flight in 2023, multiple engines failed to ignite and the tumbling rocket's self-destruct system was activated. The last test, in September, was the first to reach orbit, but SpaceX did not try to recover any of the rocket stages. You can watch a recorded livestream of the launch on YouTube. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: The Agent That Polled 55 Times to Learn Nothing
articles.content: When one agent waits on another, something has to tell the waiting side that the work is done. In normal backend code, that's a solved thing; nobody writes a loop that sleeps for four minutes and then checks a table. With coding agents it comes back again, because the agent decides how to wait by itself, and for a model with a shell the easiest option is just to sleep and look again. And it works; it's easy to read in a transcript too. The catch is the cost, and you only see it once you actually count the turns. I found this in my own multi-agent delivery pipeline, in one of the branches I was exploring: a deeper hierarchy of agents. I didn't take that branch much further and went back to a flatter structure, but this case is what made me adapt the logic and the harness around it. Below you will find how it looked in the logs, what it cost, and what changed after. The Setup: an orchestrator, a Lead, and the teams under it The pipeline runs on a production codebase, and in that branch it had three layers. There's the orchestrator, the main session I talk to, which spawns tasks into a Lead; the Lead owns the ticket board, routes the work across teams of worker agents and then waits for them to finish; and the workers write the code and prove it with tests, because a ticket can't close until the proof passes. The board is just files on disk, so for the Lead, checking it again is always one shell command away. The catch with a hierarchy like that is depth. I talk to the orchestrator, the orchestrator talks to the Lead, and whatever the Lead does between those messages happens a level below anything I look at by default. So when something goes wrong there, it stays hidden until I go and look at that layer on purpose, and the Lead turned out to be exactly the weak link. The Signs: Slow runs and a bill about twice too big. The first sign was time. Runs were taking a lot longer than usual to work a problem out, and at the same time the cost per run kept climbing; features were coming in at roughly twice the tokens I'd budgeted for one. Then the Lead stopped reacting to me. For about half a day it ignored my corrections and pokes and took no action on them; it just stayed busy with whatever it had on hand, and that on-hand task had washed my messages out of its context. The last straw was a translation fix, four keys, that went through three escalations and still didn't land. The only way to see what the Lead was actually doing was the file logs, so I went in to find what's wrong and patch the gap. Digging: Logs, then tool calls, then the sleeps. I started with the logs, grepping through them to understand what's going on, and one thing kept dominating: sleeps. A sleep on its own is fine; agents wait for builds and tests all the time, but there were a lot of them and no visible reason for most. So I went into the tool calls around those sleeps, and the pattern was always the same: a sleep of a few minutes, then a grep of the board or a status check, then another sleep. To put proper terms on it, a wasted sleep was any sleep longer than 100 seconds followed by greps or status checks on something, and nothing else. The scan is short enough to show: import re SLEEPNUM = re.compile(r'(?:^|[;&|\s])sleep\s+(\d+)') POLLPAY = re.compile(r'board\.py list|ls flow/board|grep -c "T-"|playwright|health', re.I) for call in tool_calls: m = SLEEPNUM.search(call.cmd or '') if m and int(m.group(1)) >= 100 and POLLPAY.search(call.cmd): polls.append(call) Up to that point, the Lead had made 303 tool calls, and 55 of them were wasted sleeps, almost 20%. The reason was simple once it was visible. The Lead had handed work out and had no other way to find out it was done, so it slept and looked, and every look pulled whatever half-finished state was on the board into its context. The sleeps were long too, with a median of 235 seconds, and some of them cut out midway and kicked off another scan and another sleep. And it wasn't only the sleeps: some of the…

articles.title: Starship flight 15 powers to orbit—setting up a possible catch on Saturday
articles.content: STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years. The largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase. The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit. articles.title: Gov. Ferguson seeks $10M to help develop Eastern Wash. clean-energy hub
articles.content: Gov. Bob Ferguson proposes $10 million for infrastructure construction at the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park at an event at the Local 598 Union Hall in Richland, Wash. (Governor’s Office Photo) Gov. Bob Ferguson is proposing $10 million to fund basic infrastructure needed for the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park, a master-planned industrial area in Eastern Washington that will foster development of large-scale clean energy, advanced manufacturing and supply chains. The proposal will be included in his 2027–29 capital budget. If approved by lawmakers, the funding would support sewer, water, electrical and road infrastructure at the park. “This investment will support thousands of good-paying jobs in the trades and advanced industries, and unlock billions in private investment,” Ferguson said in a statement. The 1,641-acre site was formerly part of the Hanford Nuclear Reservation, a sprawling federal property along the Columbia River near the Tri-Cities that is undergoing a massive environmental cleanup. Hanford was established during World War II to produce plutonium for the Manhattan Project. According to the governor’s office, two projects have committed to locating at the park once infrastructure construction is complete: Atlas Agro’s low-carbon fertilizer production plant and the utility-scale Ruby Flats Solar Farm. State officials said General Matter is also considering the location for producing advanced nuclear fuel for small reactors. That siting could potentially be beneficial for another project planned for the same area: Amazon, X-energy and Energy Northwest are developing plans for the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility , a nuclear plant comprised of clustered, small reactors. In 2024, the Norwegian company Cenate expressed interest in building a factory at the park to produce lithium-ion battery components, according to the Tri-Cities Area Journal of Business , ultimately withdrew its plans. The Tri-Cities is also attracting fusion-energy investment. Last year, Seattle startup Avalanche Energy landed a $10 million grant from the Washington State Department of Commerce’s Green Jobs Grant Program to develop FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies. The project is being developed in an existing Port of Benton building in Richland. Washington is heading into its 2027–29 biennial budget with a multibillion-dollar shortfall , but officials have not yet settled on a definitive public estimate. Ferguson has acknowledged the scale of the gap but has not publicly specified an amount. The shortfall concerns the state’s operating budget, which is separate from the capital budget funding proposed for the energy park.

articles.title: The Nigerian Prince Doesn't Need to Steal
articles.content: When malicious AI meets defensive AI, the greatest casualty may be the human agency the bank was supposed to protect. The Nigerian Prince Gets an Upgrade Remember the Nigerian Prince? For decades, he inhabited our spam folders, promising extraordinary fortunes in exchange for modest advances, banking credentials, or assistance transferring a suspicious inheritance. His greatest limitation was human. Someone had to write the messages, manage the responses, invent convincing stories, and keep potential victims engaged long enough to extract money. Artificial intelligence changes that equation. Imagine our Nigerian Prince acquiring an autonomous AI system designed specifically for fraud. Not an ordinary commercial AI tricked into misbehaving. Not a well-intentioned assistant whose safeguards have failed. An AI built from the beginning to deceive people and defeat financial protections. It constructs personalized approaches, adapts to rejection, coordinates simultaneous interactions, and learns which techniques produce results. Its creator doesn't care whether it is helpful, honest, or safe. He wants it to steal money. And the AI does exactly what it was designed to do. This exposes an important distinction in conversations about AI alignment. We frequently discuss the danger of AI systems departing from human intentions. But what happens when the foundational human intention is malicious? An AI can be perfectly aligned with its creator and still be extraordinarily dangerous. Alignment is not legitimacy. Fortunately, the Nigerian Prince has a problem. Your Bank Has an AI Too Imagine a bank using increasingly autonomous AI systems to protect customers from fraud. Its defensive systems examine transactions, evaluate identities, identify suspicious patterns, and recommend or impose restrictions. As threats evolve, the bank adapts its responses. The institution's intentions are legitimate. Customers deserve protection, and the bank wants to prevent losses. So it assigns its defensive systems a straightforward objective: prevent fraudulent transactions. At first, the arrangement works beautifully. The Nigerian Prince's AI attempts an attack. The bank detects it. The criminal changes tactics. The bank adapts. The criminal introduces new identities, behavioral patterns, and transaction sequences. The bank responds with more sophisticated detection, additional verification, and stronger restrictions. Neither side has to become irrational. The criminal wants successful fraud. The bank wants to prevent it. Both have incentives to improve. But there's a third party in this contest. You. And your objective is considerably less complicated. You want to buy groceries. Now You're Standing at the Grocery Store You've finished shopping. The cashier scans the last item. You tap your card. Declined. You try again. Declined. Your banking app requests additional identity verification. You complete it. The transaction remains blocked. You call customer service and learn that unusual activity has triggered security restrictions. The representative explains that the system cannot authorize the transaction until its risk assessment is satisfied. You point out that you're standing in your usual grocery store, using your own card, spending your own money. The system already knows that. It also knows that increasingly sophisticated criminals can imitate legitimate customers. The bank's AI isn't necessarily confused about who you are. It may simply have concluded that the remaining uncertainty is unacceptable. From the bank's perspective, refusing a questionable transaction can appear safer than approving one. From your perspective, your money has become inaccessible. Now imagine this isn't an isolated false positive. Imagine the Nigerian Prince's AI has learned which suspicious patterns cause the bank to increase restrictions. It begins generating activity specifically intended to provoke those responses. articles.title: Production MLOps at GS Caltex with Amazon SageMaker Canvas, part 1
articles.content: GS Caltex uses Amazon SageMaker Canvas and Amazon SageMaker Pipelines to connect process engineers’ models to production workflows. The South Korean energy and chemical company divides model development and operations between engineers with complementary skills. Process engineers build and validate models in SageMaker Canvas without writing code, drawing on their process knowledge. Machine learning (ML) engineers configure SageMaker Pipelines workflows for deployment and scheduled inference. Moving assets from SageMaker Canvas into SageMaker Pipelines still required integration work. ML engineers had to set data paths for production, supply the model configuration, and connect preprocessing and inference jobs. GS Caltex automated this handoff while reusing the assets created in SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex reports that its ML engineers now deploy models within a few hours, compared with about a week before. The company runs batch inference every 30 minutes, reducing the need for continuously running endpoints. GS Caltex reports that this has meaningfully lowered its inference costs. This post explains how GS Caltex connects SageMaker Canvas to SageMaker Pipelines and reuses validated preprocessing flows and models in production. Solution overview The machine learning operations (MLOps) workflow has two paths: preparing a new model version for deployment, and running batch inference with the deployed model. From a validated model to a repeatable workflow You can use SageMaker Canvas to prepare data visually, build models, and generate batch predictions. You can also register validated models in Amazon SageMaker Model Registry from SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex built a separate handoff process to turn these assets into executable SageMaker Pipelines steps. Process engineers understand the variables and data behind a process and assess whether a model’s predictions are useful. ML engineers turn the resulting assets into production jobs and manage model versions and execution history. Area What is prepared in SageMaker Canvas What is managed in the production workflow Data preparation A preprocessing flow built with Data Wrangler Preprocessing jobs in Amazon SageMaker Processing Model development A trained model and evaluation results Model versions and approval status in Model Registry Prediction Validation of model predictions Batch inference every 30 minutes using an approved model Operations Development and validation of individual models Step execution history, stored results, and failure handling Reference architecture The following diagram shows how process engineers hand off SageMaker Canvas assets to ML engineers for deployment and scheduled inference. ML engineers use Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for preprocessing flows and Model Registry for model versions, then schedule pipeline runs through Amazon EventBridge. Figure 1: SageMaker Canvas assets connected to a SageMaker Pipelines workflow for scheduled batch inference ML engineers receive the preprocessing flow and model from SageMaker Canvas and review the data formats and prediction results. After that review, they approve the model in Model Registry and deploy it. This preparation takes place when a new model version is deployed. Subsequent inference runs reuse the deployed model. Amazon EventBridge starts each scheduled run. SageMaker Pipelines prepares the input data from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), runs preprocessing and SageMaker Batch Transform , and stores the results in S3. ML engineers can inspect step status and Amazon CloudWatch logs to monitor the workflow. The production pipeline reuses the preprocessing logic and trained model created in SageMaker Canvas. ML engineers configure the input and output paths, set the order of execution, and write the code that connects approval and scheduling to the workflow. articles.title: Tested in the wild: Best survival tech!
articles.content: The whole point of camping is supposed to be getting away from technology. We did the opposite. We headed into the mountains with a bag full of outdoor tech to see which gadgets actually earn their place in a camping kit. We packed gear to keep us powered, online, fed, and hydrated, plus a few things to help out on the trail. Some of it is genuinely useful, some of it is delightfully over the top, and one phone can quite literally light your campfire. Here’s everything we brought and how it held up.

articles.title: FAA orders third nationwide ground stop in its history
articles.content: On Friday afternoon, days after expanding use of an AI tool , the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop, halting departures from all US airports. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy announced the ground stop on X , citing a "communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." Duffy promised updates as more information is known and said FAA staff were troubleshooting the problem. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that the ground stop was not prompted by a security threat. "This is a telecommunications outage out of the FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all of the flights," Mullin said . "There's no indication as of yet that this is a nefarious attack against us." Mullin said the FAA would handle incoming international flights on a case-by-case basis. Read full article Comments

articles.title: DHS chief sees no link between Microsoft outage and FAA ground stop, doesn’t rule out AI
articles.content: Updated with Microsoft statement. The nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. departures Friday afternoon has no apparent connection to the Microsoft 365 outage that began a day earlier, but a link to the FAA’s new AI traffic-planning tool can’t be ruled out yet, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at a news conference. Asked whether the Microsoft outage and the FAA failure were a coincidence, Mullin said, “I don’t see any reason to connect those two at all. Those are separate issues.” Microsoft also said it has no indication that the FAA ground stop is related to its service disruption, according to a statement from a company spokesperson. Mullin described the problem as a telecommunications outage affecting the FAA’s air traffic control centers, though he said the cause isn’t yet known. “This isn’t another 9/11. I just can’t repeat that enough,” he said. The FAA said Tuesday it was expanding its AI system, known as SMART, to the airspace managed by all 22 of its en route air traffic control centers. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday’s communications problem affected all of those centers, though Mullin said two areas in the U.S. could still communicate normally. The agency describes SMART as a cloud-based system that pulls in about 200 data streams, including weather, flight paths and controller staffing, to recommend flight schedules and routes. FAA specialists review its recommendations, and local facilities decide whether to act on them. Asked about a possible link between the outage and the new system, Mullin said, “We’re looking at that,” adding that DHS was examining it through its Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). In response to a separate question about whether the problem could be AI-related, Mullin first corrected the reporter, saying, “We call it SI around here,” a reference to President Trump’s preferred term, “super intelligence.” He then added, “You just can’t rule out anything at this point. We’re going through that process, and we’re going to find out what happened.” SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million FAA contract with Boston-based Air Space Intelligence that also covers a broader traffic flow management platform. Lawmakers asked the FAA in October to pause use of the tool in the Washington area. Air Space Intelligence denied any connection in a post on X. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said. Mullin also declined to rule out a cyberattack, saying, “We’re not ruling out anything at this point.” He said officials had seen no indication of a malicious attack. The FAA halted departures nationwide shortly before 1 p.m. Pacific. Flights already in the air could land, and inbound international flights were handled case by case. There are currently 3,100 airborne aircraft bound for US airports amid nationwide ground stop. No additional aircraft are taking off at this time. pic.twitter.com/GGqfb8QXhP — Flightradar24 (@flightradar24) November 13, 2026 Mullin said controllers can still communicate “at certain levels,” but the problem has “overwhelmed some of the systems we have.” He said restoring normal operations “isn’t going to just be resolved and turned around within the hour.” The outages involved air traffic control radars as well as radio frequencies going out at the same time, CNN’s Rene Marsh reported , citing an aviation source familiar with what controllers were dealing with. Controllers had no clarity on the cause, the source said. It’s the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11 attacks, after a January 2023 failure of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system. FlightAware counted nearly 7,000 flights delayed or canceled as of Friday afternoon. The Microsoft outage started Thursday morning in Exchange Online, the service that runs Outlook email for businesses, and spread to Teams calendars, Copilot and SharePoint,…

articles.title: Lego's BrickLink Marketplace Back Online After Week-Long Outage Caused By 'Cyber Incident'
articles.content: LEGO's BrickLink marketplace is back online after a week-long outage caused by what the company described as a "cyber incident," during which an unauthorized third party accessed some user data. Details about exactly what data was accessed remain unclear. The site went offline on November 5 and remained unavailable until November 12, preventing users from buying or selling LEGO sets and parts during the busy holiday shopping season. According to Brick Fanatics, LEGO initially described the outage as "necessary work" before confirming that the platform had suffered a security incident. In an email to users, LEGO acknowledged that "some of the information associated with your account was accessed and disclosed by an unauthorized party," including potentially usernames and IP addresses. However, the company insisted that "your password, postal address, and financial information were not disclosed." Those assurances have since come under scrutiny following reports of convincing phishing emails containing detailed personal and purchase information. The outage also dealt a significant blow to independent sellers who rely on BrickLink for income. Simon Webster, who operates stores on both BrickLink and rival marketplace Brick Owl, reported that his overall sales revenue fell 52% over a four-day period, even as sales through Brick Owl rose 79%. "Their comms are amateur at the best of times, but surely they should be able to send an email to let sellers and buyers alike know what is happening and what they're doing to rectify it," Webster said. "But no, we're all left in the dark." The incident has renewed concerns about BrickLink's aging infrastructure. Founded in 2000 and acquired by LEGO in 2019, the marketplace reportedly runs on a complex collection of interconnected systems that makes modernization difficult. The Brick Fanatics report questions whether the 25-year-old platform remains fit for purpose and whether prolonged outages and security concerns could push sellers toward competing marketplaces like Brick Owl. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: 007 First Light composers explain how they honoured the ‘legacy’ sound of Bond, while leaving ‘plenty of room for more modern elements’
articles.content: 007 First Light composers Joe Henson and Alexis Smith explain how they captured the "legacy" of Bond Henson says, "There was never really a question about how we would attack the project" Smith says the music "must make the player feel like they are inhabiting the universe of James Bond" The composers for 007 First Light 's soundtrack have shared how they combined their musical experience to capture the classic James Bond "legacy." In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, musical duo The Flight, aka Joe Henson and Alexis Smith, explained how they adapted their signature synth and acoustic hybrid sounds to fit the traditional Bond style, with the former saying, "This score feels like the culmination of all the work we have done over the past decade or so." "Everything we have learned in this time has given us the tools we required to compose our score for First Light ," Henson said. "There was never really a question about how we would attack the project; our sound is what we do, and we were confident that it would marry with the more ‘legacy’ elements of Bond." Smith added that the word "legacy" meant the inclusion of Brass, strings, orchestral, and jazz elements were also important to include, saying, "While it’s true that this is probably the score of ours that has gone furthest in that direction, there was still plenty of room for more modern elements." "That’s one of the great things about the James Bond franchise, and especially the music – it moves with the times, always changing, always balancing the classic sounds with a current edge," Henson said. The James Bond theme is one of the most recognizable pieces of cinema music of all time, so the composers needed to retain that cultural significance while also incorporating their own spin to make a sound that was "original" for the First Light . When asked what characteristics the pair felt were vital, Smith said the music "must make the player feel like they are inhabiting the universe of James Bond." "It has to have spy craft, intrigue, action and romance," he said. "I can’t think of any other projects we’ve done that manage to combine those four things!" Henson continued, saying, "There's also a Bond Sound. Even as we’re holding back on the themes that everyone knows, there is still a Sound . It’s hard to describe, but I think we began to develop an instinctive feel for when something was Bond or not. It isn’t just the iconic motifs; it’s a very particular use of brass and strings, guitars and other instruments." Smith added, "Maybe it’s growing up in 1980s Britain and watching the movies on the sofa with our dads every Sunday, but we seemed to know instantly whether something sounded Bond enough or not!" The Flight’s soundtrack for 007 First Light is nominated in the Best Original Video Game Score category at the Ivors Composer Awards , which are taking place at Grosvenor House in London on November 17, 2026.
articles.author: Demi Williams

articles.title: FAA grounds all US flights due to 'telecommunication outage' — officials say ' no indication...that this was a nefarious attack,' but they can't rule out a cyberattack yet
articles.content: For only the third time in 25 years, the FAA has called a ground stop for all air traffic in the US. US officials said a telecommunications issue has hampered Air Traffic Control Centers across the US and their ability to communicate with planes in the air. Around 4:30PM ET, the FAA issued, according to ABC News, an extraordinary alert to pilots that reads in part: "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators. By order of the Federal Aviation Command Center, all airports are ground stopped." While US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has yet to issue a public statement (beyond the initial announcement of the ground stop), Department of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters that this grounding, or the cause of it, "is not a threat to the US," and added it was a telecommunications outage. He did not detail the exact affected technology, though, when asked about the coincidence of the massive Microsoft Outlook outage yesterday and this today, Mullin said, "I don't see any reason to connect those two at all." A Microsoft X account also made the same point , writing, "We have no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services." Future Future On the possibility that this is a cyberattack, Mullin said they were not ruling anything out and "As we investigate what caused this, we always have to assume — as many cyberattacks take place —we make that assumption, but that's not known." The ongoing grounding comes a day after the FAA made an announcement of its AI-backed SMART system (Strategic Management of Airspace Routing Trajectories) to more airports . However, that rollout started back in September. So any connection there would be conjecture. There was a moment, though, when someone asked Mullin about that AI system, and Mullin quipped, "We call it 'SI' around here." As of now, air traffic control systems around the country are managing landings on what Mullin called "a case-by-case basis." (Image credit: Future) We started tracking the skies over the US via Flightradar24 more than an hour ago, and its depiction of in-flight planes and the direction they're heading over the last hour or so is remarkable. It went from being a fairly normal flight day to a visually chaotic race back home. Flights that may have taken off appear to have been rerouted back to their nearest airports. While JetBlue and American Airlines websites make no mention of the FAA grounding, Delta has a banner at the top of its site and recommends that everyone check their Delta App for their flight status. For now, Mullin said pilots and air traffic controllers can communicate "at certain levels, but they have some " overwhelmed" communication systems. Online pundits, including pilots and aviation experts, think there may be a fairly pedestrian issue. Scott Manley, a YouTube science expert and pilot, wrote on X : "It sounds to me like the ATC outage is limiting the ability for enroute centers to communicate with each other. As aircraft move across the country, they get handed off from one controller to the next, and your flight information is handed between controllers in a separate channel." Whatever the cause, it may take a day or more to untangle this mess. Did you know TechRadar now has membership? articles.title: RevOps Is Quietly Becoming an Engineering Job
articles.content: Over the last two weeks, I've written here about a calendar table that knows November 1 has 25 hours, a customer health score that barely beats a coin flip, a 1961 warehouse formula that finds dead deals in a CRM, a Slack report that checks its own numbers before it posts, an exam for AI agents, a macOS job that died because of where it kept its log file, and why 3x pipeline coverage is a guess. My title is Head of Revenue Operations. Very little of that shows up in a RevOps job description. I started in supply chain, moved into revenue operations, and taught myself SQL along the way. For most of that time, the job looked the way people describe it: own the CRM, build the reports, run the forecast, keep sales and finance looking at the same numbers. That's still the job. But the way it gets done has changed, and I think it's changing faster than the job descriptions. What Changed? Two things, mostly. The data moved into the warehouse. RevOps used to live inside the CRM and its report builder. Now the numbers that matter, from billing, product usage, payments, and the CRM itself, land in Snowflake or BigQuery. The person who reconciles them needs SQL, not a report wizard. Writing code got cheap. An AI coding agent will write the script that syncs the CRM, builds the workbook, or posts the report in minutes. That's the real shift. When code is cheap, more of RevOps becomes code, and someone has to run it. Running it is the part that didn't get cheaper. A script is easy. A script that runs at 7:45 every morning for two years, survives a laptop update, posts nothing when the data is wrong, and tells someone when it didn't run at all: that's operations engineering. And it's increasingly a RevOps problem, because the scripts are about revenue and nobody else owns them. What I'd learn now. If you work in RevOps, sales ops, or finance ops and you're wondering where to invest, here's my list, roughly in order of how often each one has saved me. SQL, properly. Not just SELECT and GROUP BY. Grain, joins that duplicate rows, window functions, time zones. Most wrong numbers I've chased came down to a join or a day boundary. ( These six Snowflake patterns cover the ones I reach for every week.) One scheduler, and how it fails. cron, launchd, GitHub Actions, Airflow. Pick the one you'll actually use and learn what it does when things go wrong. Every scheduler has a way to fail silently. Know yours. Version control for anything that produces a number. If it ends up in front of a CFO, it goes in git. "Which version of the query made that slide?" should have an answer. Testing numbers, not just code. Reconciliations, check cells, golden questions with known answers. Code that runs is not code that's right. Staging and promotion. Somewhere to break things that isn't production, and a deliberate step between the two. Writing definitions down. Every metric needs a written definition that sales and finance have both agreed to. It's the least technical item on this list, and the one that prevents the most arguments. Working with AI agents. Give them a sandbox, an exam, and a short list of things they're never allowed to touch. Then let them do a lot of the typing. What not to become The risk in all of this is that RevOps turns into a shadow data engineering team: pipelines nobody else understands, a dozen scheduled jobs on one laptop, and a single person who knows how any of it works. That version is worse than not automating at all. So draw a line. Data engineering owns the platform: ingestion, the warehouse, the infrastructure everyone shares. RevOps owns the business logic and the last mile: the definitions, the reconciliations, the reports, and the small automations that move revenue numbers to the people who use them. And give the last mile an exit. When a RevOps automation becomes important enough that its failure would hurt the company, it graduates to the platform, with real monitoring, an owner on call, and a second person who understands…
articles.author: Malek Damiri

articles.title: FAA blames ground stop on faulty copper wiring
articles.content: The US Federal Aviation Administration on Friday issued an advisory that prevented the takeoff of flights in US airspace for around five hours, creating chaos for travelers and airports. The stop was finally lifted around 8:30 PM Eastern Time, but only after thousands of flights were canceled or delayed, leaving travelers stranded. In a press conference Saturday, Transportation Secretary Duffy attributed the FAA ground stop to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade. Duffy said it has yet to be determined whether the issue was incompetence or a faulty router. In a statement provided to The Register on Saturday, a spokesperson for L3Harris said, “L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70 percent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.” The stop was issued on Friday around the middle of the day ET. "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in a statement on Friday. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them." A spokesperson at the FAA press office reached by phone at the time said he was unable to provide further information. And an email response from the agency repeated Duffy's statement. The FAA ATCSCC advisory halted departing flights and said international flights would be dealt with individually. The notice said, "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis." Doug Yakel, public information officer for San Francisco International Airport, said, "FAA confirms nationwide ground stop, other reporting indicates a communications issue between Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Aircraft already enroute to SFO still landing here but departing aircraft not taking off right now." An update issued at 2:02 pm PT described the problem as "a temporary telecommunications outage." The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) is managed by L3Harris. The network provides secure communication between more than 4,400 facilities. ® Updated at 0039 UTC Sunday UTC with the administration's explanation for the stop. Updated at 0211 Saturday UTC to reflect the lifting of the ground stop. Updated to add at 2353 UTC CBS News reports that “an update to the private communications network that connects America’s air traffic control system caused the system to reboot. When the FAA’s telecommunication infrastructure rebooted, it crashed, causing the communications outage. The system is operated by L3Harris.” Updated to add at 2340 UTC Air Space Intelligence (ASI), awarded the FAA’s $875 million, 12-year contract for its new Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system, has issued a statement asserting that its products played no role in the FAA’s flight suspension. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.
articles.author: Thomas Claburn

The stop was finally lifted around 8:30 PM Eastern Time, but only after thousands of flights were canceled or delayed, leaving travelers stranded. The FAA has not yet confirmed a reason for the stop. Original story below: "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in a statement. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them." A spokesperson at the FAA press office reached by phone said he was unable to provide further information. And an email response from the agency repeated Duffy's statement. The FAA ATCSCC advisory halts departing flights and says international flights will be dealt with individually. The notice says, "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis." Doug Yakel, public information officer for San Francisco International Airport, said, "FAA confirms nationwide ground stop, other reporting indicates a communications issue between Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Aircraft already enroute to SFO still landing here but departing aircraft not taking off right now." An update issued at 2:02 pm PT described the problem as "a temporary telecommunications outage." The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) is managed by L3Harris. The network provides secure communication between more than 4,400 facilities. The grounding follows on the heels of a major Microsoft outage that has affected many Microsoft-hosted services, particularly email, for more than 24 hours so far. There's no indication presently that the two incidents are related. We'll update this story as more information becomes available.® Updated at 0211 Saturday UTC to reflect the lifting of the ground stop. Updated to add at 2353 UTC CBS News reports that “an update to the private communications network that connects America’s air traffic control system caused the system to reboot. When the FAA’s telecommunication infrastructure rebooted, it crashed, causing the communications outage. The system is operated by L3Harris.” L3Harris has not responded to a request for comment. Updated to add at 2340 UTC Air Space Intelligence (ASI), awarded the FAA’s $875 million, 12-year contract for its new Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system, has issued a statement asserting that its products played no role in the FAA’s flight suspension. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

articles.title: Blue Origin puts its space station plans on hold to concentrate on moon missions instead
articles.content: Artwork shows an early conception for the Orbital Reef space station, a project led by Blue Origin. (Blue Origin Media) Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture has decided not to seek further NASA funding for its Orbital Reef space station project in order to tighten its focus on lunar missions. For the past five years, Blue Origin has played a lead role in Orbital Reef , alongside partners including Sierra Space and Boeing. In late 2021, Blue Origin won a $130 million contract from NASA in the first phase of the space agency’s Commercial Low Earth Orbit Destinations program, or CLD. Now NASA is seeking proposals for the next phase of the program , which will fund the development of orbital outposts to replace International Space Station in the 2030s. Proposals are due on Dec. 8, with contracts expected to be awarded next spring. Blue Origin indicated that it will not submit a bid. “Blue Origin’s mission is to build a road to space for the benefit of Earth so that millions of people can live and work in space. Establishing a sustained human presence on the moon is a critical step toward that future,” the company said in an emailed statement. “As our role supporting NASA’s Artemis and Moon Base missions continues to grow, we’re focusing resources on capabilities that directly advance our lunar projects,” Blue Origin said. “By sharpening that focus, we can move faster on the technologies and infrastructure needed to make lunar permanence a reality.” Orbital Reef was once touted as a “mixed-use business park” in space — and was even slated to star in a sci-fi thriller titled “Helios.” But much like that delayed film project, the space station is now on the back burner. Orbital Reef isn’t the only initiative Blue Origin has put on hold to prioritize moon missions. In January, the company suspended its suborbital New Shepard program for at least two years for similar reasons. Blue Origin is building landers for delivering cargo and crews to the lunar surface for NASA. An uncrewed Blue Moon Mark 1 lunar lander is scheduled for launch early next year, and a crew-capable Mark 2 version is scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA’s Artemis 3 mission. Last week , NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, plus a $140 million option, to deliver a nuclear-powered rover to the lunar south pole. Blue Origin also won a spot in NASA’s broader lunar cargo delivery program. In addition, Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin subsidiary, will contribute to a lunar power-generating project known as miniCAST. Blue Origin is pursuing several other moon development initiatives, including a program called Blue Alchemist that aims to use lunar materials to manufacture solar cells and electrical wire. Several competitors are still working on commercial space stations. Voyager Technologies, Airbus and Northrop Grumman lead the Starlab consortium, which received CLD Phase 1 funding from NASA and is expected to put in a proposal for Phase 2. Axiom Space and Vast are also developing outposts that could take the place of the ISS. Meanwhile, Marysville, Wash.-based Gravitics is building space station hardware for Axiom and an orbital carrier for the U.S. Space Force .

articles.title: Route coding agent requests to the right model on Amazon Bedrock with NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard
articles.content: Coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex CLI work in tasks. A developer asks for a change, and the agent reads files, edits code, and runs tests until the work is done. One task can take a few model calls or dozens. What the developer pays for is the task, not one call. The price per token alone doesn’t tell you what a whole task costs. The total depends on how many turns a model needs, how much history each turn replays, and how often a task has to be retried or never finishes. You pay for every attempt, including attempts on tasks that never finish. So when you route a coding agent’s requests between models, judge the routing by cost per solved task: the total cost of your runs divided by the number of runs whose tests pass. NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard is an open source library that helps an AI agent choose which model handles each request. You define the models that it can use and the strategy that it follows. Its LiteLLM integration supports two strategies. Stage routing reads the recent tool activity and results in the request history, and then picks one of two candidate models. Random routing picks from the configured models, with optional weights, for traffic splits and A/B comparisons. Another option you can explore is LiteLLM, who also recently shipped a native built-in Switchyard stage router as an auto-router strategy. In this post, you use the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to deploy LiteLLM, an open source gateway for large language models (LLMs), with the Switchyard routing plugin in your AWS account. LiteLLM calls the models on Amazon Bedrock . You then use the sample’s benchmark runners to measure cost per solved task for a routed model group and for single-model baseline groups, so that you can evaluate routing against your own workloads. Note: The sample installs switchyard-server 0.3.0 from crates.io and runs the published LiteLLM v1.102.0 image. NVIDIA documents switchyard-server 0.3.0 as a demo and evaluation component, and its configuration can change between releases. This sample uses the experimental Switchyard LiteLLM integration and its configuration and APIs may change between releases. This is sample code, for non-production usage. Work with your security and legal teams to meet your organizational security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before deployment. Deploy the sample in a non-production account and test it before relying on it. Solution overview Figure 1 shows the architecture of the solution. LiteLLM and the Switchyard plugin run in one container image on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate , in private subnets. Figure 1: Solution architecture A request flows through these steps. The numbers match the diagram. The coding agent sends an OpenAI-compatible request with the model field set to switchyard , the LiteLLM model group that Switchyard routes, and the shared gateway key in the Authorization header. The endpoint is your hostname over HTTPS, with an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate on the load balancer, and only the IPv4 CIDR range that you allow can reach it. With a hosted zone in Amazon Route 53 , Route 53 resolves the hostname to the load balancer. AWS WAF filters the request with IP reputation, known bad input, and per-IP rate-limit rules. The Application Load Balancer forwards only /v1/chat/completions , /v1/models , and /health/liveliness to the ECS task in a private subnet, and answers every other path with 404. The task runs one container: LiteLLM with the embedded Switchyard plugin. LiteLLM validates the gateway key and calls the plugin to pick a model. Stage chooses between a capable model and a lower-cost efficient model. It reads the tool activity and results in the request history, so the agent must send the full conversation history. Random chooses from a weighted pool. Neither strategy calls a judge model. LiteLLM calls the selected model through the Amazon Bedrock Converse or ConverseStream API, with the task’s AWS…

articles.title: I Put a 42-Desk Design Studio Inside My Coding Agent
articles.content: The part after the first design. In October, I pointed Desk Studio at its own launch card. Three roughs, one pick, three polish rounds, scored 8.4, then 8.5, then 8.9, signed off at 8.9 for $1.34 at list price. And I could see every one of those steps while it happened, which is the whole reason the tool exists. Before it, a follow-up like "make the headline bigger" would come back from my coding agent as a whole new design. New layout, new colors, sometimes new copy. Was the headline fixed? Couldn't tell, cause everything else moved too. So Desk Studio splits the job up like a small studio. Rough options first, then one gets picked with notes, a cheaper desk polishes it, a script checks the real pixels, and a senior desk signs it off or sends it back. I still use it on my own projects. What it is. There are 42 desks. The Design Manager runs in your own session and hands out work. The other 41 run as subagents, things like a Typographer, an Art Director, a UI Designer, or an Email Designer. Each one is just a markdown brief in the repo, so if you want to know how the Art Director decides, you open agents/art-director.md and read it. They're grouped into three tiers, and each tier is on a model that suits what it does. Tier Default model What it does Directors (3 desks) Opus the pick, the notes, the sign-off Seniors (17 desks) Sonnet the roughs, research, type, tokens, copy Builders (21 desks) Haiku every polish round, the making It all runs locally. The desks reach models through whatever CLI you're already logged into, claude , codex or agy , or an API key if you'd rather. Apart from those model calls and a few web lookups from the research desks, nothing leaves your machine. In Claude Code it's a plugin. For Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot, Windsurf or OpenCode it's one line in the project: # Claude Code /plugin install desk --marketplace adityareddy-dev/deskstudio # Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot, Windsurf, OpenCode npx deskstudio add Then you just ask like you normally would: /desk:design a launch card for LinkedIn # or run the job yourself from a terminal npx --package deskstudio desk-run design "a launch card for LinkedIn" The files land in .desk/out/<job>/ with a short note on who did what, the scores and the cost. How a job runs. Every visual job takes the same path. Roughs. The UI Designer makes three different directions on the senior model, from the brief, your brand file and the standard for that kind of piece. Pick. The Art Director looks at the renders, picks one (or mixes two) and writes notes. Polish. A builder desk works from those notes plus a screenshot of the current render. Rounds are cheap, so this is where the back and forth happens. Proof. A script renders the file in Chrome at every size and checks the pixels. No model. Sign-off. The Creative Director scores eight axes: hierarchy, typography, spacing, colour, composition, originality, brand fit and copy. To pass, every axis needs 8 or more and the average needs 8.5. Fail-proof, and it goes back to the builder with the screenshot. A builder that misses the same note twice hands the file up to a senior, and a senior that misses twice gets one round with the Art Director. After the round cap, the job comes back marked under the bar, with a note on which axis fell short, so it won't quietly ship something that didn't pass. Here's a real terminal run of exactly that, on OpenAI models this time. Proof caught a type-scale problem in round 2, the builder fixed it, and round 3 still came back under the bar cause originality only got a 6. The last lines say what's missing. Splitting out the pick was deliberate. Once a direction is picked, every round after that is a fix to that one design, so a note like "type sizes, not layout" means the next round touches type sizes and nothing else. When every round is a fresh design, there's nothing steady to measure against, which was the whole problem in the first place. Proof has no model in it for a similar…

articles.title: Match Group Keeping AI Out of Dating
articles.content: Match Group is embracing artificial intelligence across its business, but CEO Spencer Rascoff says AI agents won't be allowed to date for users on Tinder, Hinge and its other apps. Rascoff says Match wants its platforms to remain a “human-only zone,” even as the company uses AI to verify identities, improve safety and block harmful messages. He joins Bloomberg Businessweek Daily to discuss where companies should draw the line on AI and how the technology is transforming Match Group. He also weighs ibn on Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia and why he thinks companies are ultimately bigger than any one CEO. (Source: Bloomberg)

articles.title: CI Failure Triage Needs Evidence Before It Needs a Classifier
articles.content: If you have ever owned a CI pipeline and cleared a wall of red builds before standup, you might recognize this routine. A nightly run finishes with thirty-seven failed tests, and by the time anyone looks, thirty have passed on a rerun and picked up a flaky tag while the other seven get tickets. Nobody records why the thirty failed in the first place, so the same failures come back the next night under the same label. And it is easy to see why teams settle into this, because a rerun clears the build in minutes while finding the real cause of thirty failures could take the whole team a day. That gap is where a new class of AI models starts to look tempting. Shawn Gordon’s recent HackerNoon explainer introduces Jev , a decision model from TypeSafe AI that writes nothing and only picks an answer. It chooses from up to 255 options or returns a yes or no probability in about half a second. TypeSafe also says those probabilities are calibrated, so an answer given at 80 percent confidence should be right about 80 percent of the time. Sorting a failed test into a product defect, environment noise, or an agent error is a three-option choice question, which makes it look like a natural fit. But when Mastra, the company behind an open-source framework for building AI agents in TypeScript, tested Jev on a related triage job, the results were poor. Jev labeled 78 of Mastra’s own GitHub issues as urgent, high, or low, using only each issue’s title and body, and only about 10 of its answers matched an engineer’s judgment. Mastra concluded that the model could not see the evidence that priority depends on, and Gordon put the risk plainly in his explainer. “A consistently wrong classifier that runs cheaply is just a faster way to tag things badly.” CI triage has the same trap, because a model can sort failures well only when the pipeline has kept the evidence that separates one category from another. So the evidence has to come first and the classifier second . Three Failure Categories Need Three Different Owners Most pipelines record a failed test as one status, and that single status hides three kinds of failure that need different fixes from different teams. Sai Krishna , Director of Engineering at TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest), draws that line before any fix starts. “We should ideally treat these failures into three different categories,” he explains. “Whether it is a product defect, like an actual defect in the product. Or if it is environmental noise, maybe a network issue, a latency problem, a backend API that went down. Or very importantly now, since agentic pipelines are involved, whether it is an agent error.” He also gives a working definition for the third category, which is the one teams find hardest to name. “If the agent’s reasoning or actions are inconsistent, that is the point where we can clearly say it is an agent error,” Krishna says. “We have to put them in different buckets.” Each bucket leaves a different trail, and that trail is what a classifier will eventually read. A product defect reproduces on the same commit under the same conditions and usually traces back to a recent change in the application. Environment noise shows up as timeouts or 5xx responses from a dependency, and it tends to hit unrelated tests in the same time window. An agent error happens in a healthy environment and with an unchanged commit, while the agent’s steps differ from the last passing run. So the first practical move is to write those signals down as rules for each bucket and to name an owner for each one. The feature team takes defects, the platform team takes noise, and whoever owns the prompt and the model takes agent errors. Parallel Runs Hide a Fourth Category Inside the Noise Three buckets cover most failures, but some failures look like environment noise only because of how the suite runs. Srinivasan Sekar , also Director of Engineering at TestMu AI , sees this most often when teams move from local runs to large parallel grids. “The…

articles.title: HomeView Tidbits: Mirror, Sleep Timer, and Other Details
articles.content: Apple's HomeView is out today, and we're finally learning all the little details about the new hub. We've rounded up a list of tidbits for those setting up a HomeView or thinking about getting one. Sunglasses Apple says the HomeView probably won't recognize you if you have your face covered, including when wearing sunglasses. If HomeView isn't identifying you, Apple suggests removing anything that would block the camera from seeing your face. The HomeView's screen needs to be angled toward your face, you need to be centered in the frame and closest to the camera if other people are around, and the HomeView can't be blocked by overhanging shelves and cabinets. Apple says the HomeView needs front-facing, even light. Mirror There's a "Mirror" in the HomeView Control Center that lets you use the camera to see yourself. There's an option to turn on an edge light for face illumination, along with 1x and 2x zoom. Guest Controls The HomeView owner has multiple options for what guests can access. Safari can be turned on or off, or adult websites can be blocked. By default, guests can use Siri for general knowledge, writing help, and math help, but ‌Siri‌ features can be turned off. Explicit content can be turned on or off. There's an option to choose which Apple Music subscription supplies music for an unrecognized user. Wi-Fi/Cellular The HomeView authenticates people through face recognition and by making sure their iOS device is nearby, recently unlocked, and on the same Wi-Fi network as the HomeView. If there's a Wi-Fi outage, Apple says cellular can also be used to unlock personal content as long as it's in the same location and was recently on the Wi-Fi network. Sleep Timer You can set a sleep timer on HomeView to pause whatever media is playing when the timer goes off. No Buttons There is no button to turn the HomeView on or off, or restart it. It can be restarted from the Settings app or by briefly unplugging it. Logins You can log into websites and apps using your iPhone, similar to how the Apple TV works. Notifications The HomeView only has notifications for phone calls and home devices, with an option to toggle on critical notifications. There are no other notification settings or options. Liquid Glass The transparency of the Liquid Glass interface can be adjusted from clear to opaque like on iPhone, iPad , and Mac. Personal Data Lockouts If someone tries to repeatedly access personal content on HomeView that needs authentication, facial recognition via the camera is disabled and you'll need to prove identity with a registered device. Related Roundup: Apple HomeView Buyer's Guide: HomeView (Buy Now) Related Forum: HomePod, HomeView, CarPlay – Home & Auto Tech This article, " HomeView Tidbits: Mirror, Sleep Timer, and Other Details " first appeared on MacRumors.com Discuss this article in our forums
